subtopic_detail: Necrotising enterocolitis - recognition and initial management
stem: A 10-day-old male infant born at 29 weeks gestation (birth weight 1.15 kg) is being cared for in the neonatal intensive care unit. He has been receiving incremental enteral feeds of expressed breast milk via orogastric tube, currently at 120 mL/kg/day, and supplemental parenteral nutrition. Over the past 8 hours the nursing staff report increasing gastric aspirate volumes that are bilious in colour. The infant has passed two stools containing visible blood.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 62/min, SpO2 91% on 0.25 FiO2 (baseline 0.21), temperature 36.2 degrees C (axillary), capillary refill 4 seconds centrally
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with visible loops, tender on palpation with erythema of abdominal wall, decreased bowel sounds, lethargy and reduced spontaneous movements
data_table.Investigations: WCC 3.2 x10^9/L, platelets 78 x10^9/L, CRP 86 mg/L, blood gas pH 7.24 pCO2 48 mmHg BE -8, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, AXR shows diffuse pneumatosis intestinalis with no free air

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Reduce enteral feeds to trophic volumes only
Cease feeds, start IV antibiotics, decompress gut
Arrange urgent laparotomy for bowel resection
Switch to extensively hydrolysed formula feeds
Transfer for urgent gastrointestinal contrast study

subtopic_detail: Recurrent croup - investigation for structural cause
stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with her fifth episode of croup in the past 12 months. Each episode has presented with barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and mild respiratory distress, and has responded promptly to a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg. She has no history of endotracheal intubation or previous airway procedures. Between episodes she has been well with no stridor at rest, normal voice, and normal growth. She was born at term via uncomplicated delivery. She has no history of atopy or recurrent wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, RR 34/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C, weight 11.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Intermittent barking cough, mild inspiratory stridor at rest, mild subcostal recession, no drooling or dysphagia, oropharynx normal, chest clear on auscultation bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Previous CXR (3 months ago): normal subglottic region, no mass lesion, normal cardiac silhouette

lead_in: After treating this acute episode, what is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Continue dexamethasone as needed per episode
Commence a trial of inhaled corticosteroids
Arrange microlaryngobronchoscopy under GA
Request a computed tomography scan of the chest
Refer for comprehensive skin prick allergy testing

subtopic_detail: Parapneumonic effusion - chest drain with fibrinolytics
stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 7-day history of cough, fever, and progressive right-sided chest pain. He was commenced on IV flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone 48 hours ago for community-acquired pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion. Despite this, he remains febrile with temperatures to 39.4 degrees C, has increased work of breathing, and reports worsening pleuritic pain. He was previously well with no significant medical history and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138 bpm, RR 36/min, SpO2 93% in room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C, weight 22 kg
data_table.Examination: Decreased air entry right lower and middle zones, dullness to percussion right hemithorax to angle of scapula, reduced chest expansion on right, no mediastinal shift clinically
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 245 mg/L, CXR large right-sided pleural effusion with opacification to mid-zone, pleural ultrasound shows septations and echogenic fluid estimated 450 mL, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue current IV antibiotics for a further 48 hours
Broaden antibiotic cover to meropenem monotherapy
Obtain CT chest with IV contrast for evaluation
Insert chest drain and instil intrapleural fibrinolytic
Proceed to video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery now

stem: A 7-month-old boy presents with 7 days of fever to 39.8 degrees C that has not responded to oral amoxicillin prescribed by his general practitioner. He has been increasingly irritable and feeding poorly. On examination he has bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection and cracked, erythematous lips. He does not have cervical lymphadenopathy, rash, or extremity changes. Blood cultures and urine culture are negative. An echocardiogram has been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 42/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C, weight 8.1 kg
data_table.Examination: Irritable and difficult to console, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, erythematous cracked lips, no rash, no extremity swelling or desquamation, no cervical lymphadenopathy, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: CRP 128 mg/L, ESR 72 mm/hr, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, platelets 520 x10^9/L, albumin 24 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, sodium 133 mmol/L, haemoglobin 98 g/L, urine microscopy sterile pyuria (25 WCC per HPF), echocardiogram shows left anterior descending coronary artery Z-score 2.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days
Continue observation and repeat bloods in 48 hours
Start oral prednisolone at 2 mg/kg/day for 14 days
Administer IV methylprednisolone pulse at 30 mg/kg
Give IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin

subtopic_detail: Neonatal HSV exposure - first-episode maternal genital herpes
stem: A term female neonate is now 12 hours old following an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The mother presented in spontaneous labour and delivered before any concerns were raised. Postnatally, the mother reports painful vulval lesions that appeared 3 days ago. She has no prior history of genital herpes. Examination of the mother confirms multiple vesicular and ulcerative vulval lesions consistent with primary genital herpes. HSV-2 PCR from a maternal lesion swab has been sent. The neonate has been breastfeeding well and appears clinically well on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142 bpm, RR 44/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, weight 3.52 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert and active, normal tone and reflexes, no vesicles or skin lesions, fontanelles soft and flat, abdomen soft, feeding well, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Maternal bloods: HSV-1 IgG negative, HSV-2 IgG negative (confirming first episode), neonate bloods not yet taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this neonate?

options.text: Start IV aciclovir and send neonatal HSV PCR
Observe with 4-hourly clinical reviews for 48 hours
Give oral valaciclovir to mother and monitor infant
Take neonatal surface swabs and await the results
Discharge home with outpatient review in 3 days

subtopic_detail: Coeliac disease serology with IgA deficiency
stem: A 3-year-old girl is referred by her general practitioner for investigation of chronic loose stools and poor weight gain over the past 9 months. She has crossed down from the 50th to the 15th centile for weight. Her diet includes regular bread, pasta, and cereals. Her mother has type 1 diabetes. Initial coeliac serology was requested and has returned. The GP is uncertain how to interpret the results given the low total IgA level.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, RR 24/min, temperature 36.7 degrees C, weight 12.4 kg (15th centile, previously 50th), height 95 cm (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Mildly distended abdomen, no hepatosplenomegaly, reduced subcutaneous fat over buttocks, no skin rash, no oral ulcers, otherwise normal examination
data_table.Investigations: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA: 8 U/mL (reference less than 15 U/mL - negative), total serum IgA: 0.05 g/L (reference 0.20-1.00 g/L - markedly low), full blood count: haemoglobin 105 g/L, MCV 68 fL, ferritin 8 mcg/L, coeliac HLA typing not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Proceed directly to upper GI endoscopy and biopsy
Request deamidated gliadin peptide IgG antibodies
Repeat tTG-IgA serology again in 3 months' time
Commence a gluten-free diet trial for 6 weeks
Send HLA DQ2 and DQ8 genotyping as next step

subtopic_detail: Acute liver failure - initial priority investigations
stem: A 4-year-old previously well boy presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of vomiting, lethargy, and progressive jaundice. His parents report he has had no recent travel, no known ingestions, and no medications other than occasional paracetamol for recent fevers. He has no significant medical history and immunisations are up to date. On examination he is jaundiced with mild confusion and intermittent agitation, which his parents say is not his usual behaviour.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 28/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C, weight 17 kg
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced sclerae and skin, liver palpable 3 cm below costal margin and tender, no splenomegaly, mild asterixis on outstretched hands, no ascites, no spider naevi, no peripheral oedema, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: ALT 4500 U/L, AST 3800 U/L, bilirubin 180 mcmol/L (conjugated 120 mcmol/L), INR 3.2, albumin 26 g/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, creatinine 52 mcmol/L, ammonia 95 mcmol/L, FBC haemoglobin 118 g/L platelets 156 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation priority?

options.text: Start N-acetylcysteine infusion before any testing
Arrange urgent percutaneous liver biopsy under sedation
Send paracetamol level, hepatitis serology, metabolic screen
Initiate therapeutic plasmapheresis for coagulopathy
Arrange immediate transfer to a transplant centre

stem: A 5-year-old boy was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome 7 weeks ago after presenting with periorbital oedema and frothy urine. He was commenced on prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day (BSA 0.78 m2) for the initial 4 weeks, then transitioned to alternate-day dosing at 40 mg/m2 for the subsequent 3 weeks as per standard protocol. Despite completing this course, he continues to have nephrotic-range proteinuria on early morning urine samples and persistent hypoalbuminaemia. He has not had any intercurrent infections. His renal function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 bpm, RR 20/min, BP 105/68 mmHg, temperature 36.6 degrees C, weight 22 kg (dry weight 19 kg)
data_table.Examination: Moderate periorbital and pedal oedema, mild abdominal distension with shifting dullness, no skin rash, no arthritis, cushingoid facies from steroid use
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 680 mg/mmol (reference less than 20), albumin 16 g/L, cholesterol 12.8 mmol/L, creatinine 38 mcmol/L, eGFR greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2, C3 and C4 normal, ANA negative, anti-dsDNA negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Extend prednisolone course for a further 4 weeks
Commence oral cyclophosphamide for 12 weeks now
Start a calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus
Arrange renal biopsy before further immunosuppression
Administer pulse IV methylprednisolone for 3 days

subtopic_detail: Typical HUS - supportive management and dialysis
stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with pallor and reduced urine output over the past 24 hours. Five days ago she developed bloody diarrhoea, which has now resolved. A stool sample sent by her GP has returned positive for Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli. She has been drinking small amounts but her parents report only one wet nappy in the past 18 hours. She appears pale and lethargic but is not in respiratory distress.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 bpm, RR 30/min, BP 118/82 mmHg (above 95th centile for age), SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, weight 14.8 kg
data_table.Examination: Pale, mildly lethargic but rousable and interactive, no petechiae or purpura, mild periorbital puffiness, abdomen soft and non-tender, no hepatosplenomegaly, no signs of fluid overload in lungs
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 68 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, blood film shows schistocytes and fragmented red cells, reticulocytes 6.8%, LDH 2800 U/L, haptoglobin less than 0.1 g/L, creatinine 280 mcmol/L (reference 20-40), urea 24 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, urine output 0.3 mL/kg/hr over 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Commence IV antibiotics for Shiga-toxin E. coli
Administer eculizumab infusion as soon as possible
Begin urgent plasma exchange via central venous access
Start empiric IV methylprednisolone at 10 mg/kg
Begin supportive care and arrange for dialysis access

subtopic_detail: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) - urgency of treatment
stem:
A 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who report clusters of sudden flexion movements of the arms and legs occurring on waking each morning for the past 2 weeks. Each cluster lasts 5 to 10 minutes with individual spasms occurring every few seconds. His parents also report that he has stopped babbling and no longer reaches for toys.

He was previously developing normally. He was born at term with no perinatal complications. On examination he is alert but has poor visual engagement and reduced spontaneous movements. An EEG is performed urgently and shows a chaotic high-amplitude pattern with disorganised slow waves and multifocal spikes consistent with hypsarrhythmia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 32, Temp 36.8 degrees C, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, poor visual tracking, reduced tone, no dysmorphic features, no neurocutaneous stigmata on Wood lamp examination
data_table.Investigations: EEG: hypsarrhythmia, FBE and UEC: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence vigabatrin immediately while arranging further workup
Start sodium valproate as first-line anticonvulsant therapy
Arrange MRI brain before commencing any medical treatment
Observe the child and arrange a repeat EEG in two weeks
Commence low-dose oral prednisolone as initial monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Childhood absence epilepsy - first-line medication choice
stem:
A 7-year-old girl is referred by her school teacher who has noticed her having multiple episodes per day of staring blankly for 5 to 10 seconds during class. She does not fall or have any limb jerking during these episodes and resumes her activity immediately afterwards with no post-ictal confusion. Her parents confirm similar episodes at home, often occurring during mealtimes.

She has no history of febrile convulsions, developmental delay, or learning difficulties. There is no family history of epilepsy. On examination she is neurologically normal. Hyperventilation for 3 minutes in the clinic provokes a typical episode with eyelid flutter and unresponsiveness lasting 8 seconds. An EEG is obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, RR 20, Temp 36.6 degrees C, BP 98/60 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no dysmorphic features, developmentally age-appropriate
data_table.Investigations: EEG: 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation, normal background. MRI brain: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medication for this child?

options.text: Commence carbamazepine as initial anticonvulsant therapy
Commence ethosuximide as initial anticonvulsant therapy
Commence sodium valproate as initial anticonvulsant therapy
Commence levetiracetam as initial anticonvulsant therapy
Commence lamotrigine as initial anticonvulsant therapy

subtopic_detail: BECTS (benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes) - management decision
stem:
An 8-year-old boy is referred to the paediatric neurology clinic after two episodes of nocturnal seizures over the past 6 months. His mother describes being woken by gurgling noises and finding him with right-sided facial twitching, drooling, and inability to speak. Each episode lasted approximately 2 minutes and resolved spontaneously. He was alert and oriented immediately afterwards but reported tingling in his tongue.

He has been well between events with no academic difficulties and is performing at the top of his class. There is no history of febrile seizures and no relevant family history. Neurological examination is entirely normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, RR 18, Temp 36.7 degrees C, BP 100/62 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, developmentally age-appropriate, no focal deficits
data_table.Investigations: EEG: high-amplitude centrotemporal spikes activated during drowsiness, normal background activity. MRI brain: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Start carbamazepine to prevent further nocturnal seizures
Start levetiracetam to prevent further nocturnal seizures
Reassure and observe, provide seizure first aid safety advice
Start sodium valproate to prevent further nocturnal seizures
Arrange a repeat MRI brain in six months for surveillance

subtopic_detail: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia - salt-wasting crisis management
stem: A 12-day-old male neonate presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of poor feeding, frequent vomiting, and progressive lethargy. He was born at 39 weeks via normal vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3.4 kg. Newborn screening results are pending. On examination he is lethargic and dehydrated with poor skin turgor and sunken fontanelle. The genitalia appear normally virilised with bilateral palpable testes. There is diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin, particularly over the areolae and genital area. Blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with pH 7.22.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 185, RR 55, Temp 36.2 degrees C, SpO2 97% on room air, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dehydrated, sunken fontanelle, diffuse hyperpigmentation, normal male genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Na 118 mmol/L, K 7.2 mmol/L, Cl 92 mmol/L, urea 8.5 mmol/L, creatinine 65 micromol/L, glucose 2.1 mmol/L, pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Administer IV dexamethasone and commence oral fludrocortisone
Commence oral sodium chloride supplementation and monitor closely
Prioritise insulin-dextrose infusion for hyperkalaemia management
Commence IV hydrocortisone and normal saline bolus with glucose
Request urgent surgical consultation for genital assessment first

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes honeymoon phase - insulin adjustment
stem:
A 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus 4 months ago and commenced on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. He presented at diagnosis with polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss but was not in diabetic ketoacidosis. His initial HbA1c was 82 mmol/mol. Over the past 3 weeks he has been experiencing frequent mild hypoglycaemic episodes, with blood glucose levels between 2.8 and 3.5 mmol/L, particularly overnight and before lunch.

His parents have already reduced his mealtime rapid-acting insulin doses. He is eating well and maintaining his usual activity level. His continuous glucose monitor shows time below range of 12% and time in range of 78%. He has no symptoms of intercurrent illness.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, RR 18, Temp 36.5 degrees C, BP 105/65 mmHg, weight 34 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, no lipohypertrophy at injection sites, no signs of other autoimmune conditions
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 38 mmol/mol, C-peptide 0.4 nmol/L (detectable), anti-GAD antibodies positive, coeliac screen negative, TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease all insulin as residual beta cell function is adequate
Commence metformin as an insulin-sparing adjunctive therapy
Increase carbohydrate intake at meals without adjusting insulin
Transition from multiple daily injections to an insulin pump
Reduce basal insulin dose by 20% and continue close monitoring

subtopic_detail: Coarctation of aorta presenting late in infancy
stem:
A 6-week-old male infant is brought to the emergency department with a 3-day history of poor feeding, sweating during feeds, and rapid breathing. He was born at term with no antenatal concerns and was discharged on day 2 of life with a normal newborn examination. On examination he is tachypnoeic with subcostal recession. His liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin.

There is a systolic murmur heard over the left sternal edge and in the interscapular region. Femoral pulses are impalpable bilaterally. Right arm blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and right leg blood pressure is 78/50 mmHg. Saturations are 98% in the right hand and 95% in the left foot.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180, RR 62, Temp 36.9 degrees C, SpO2 98% right hand, 95% left foot
data_table.Examination: Tachypnoeic, subcostal recession, 3 cm hepatomegaly, systolic murmur at left sternal edge, absent femoral pulses, BP gradient 32 mmHg upper to lower limbs
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly with pulmonary congestion. Echocardiogram: discrete coarctation of the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery with a closing ductus arteriosus, left ventricular dysfunction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence prostaglandin E1 infusion to reopen the ductus arteriosus
Schedule elective surgical repair of coarctation within the next 2 weeks
Commence oral enalapril for afterload reduction and heart failure
Observe the infant with serial echocardiograms over the next 48 hours
Commence IV furosemide and institute strict fluid restriction measures

subtopic_detail: Acute rheumatic fever - Jones criteria and secondary prophylaxis
stem:
A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from regional Queensland presents with a 1-week history of fever and painful joints. His mother reports that his knees were swollen and painful initially, then his ankles became affected as his knees improved. He had a sore throat 3 weeks ago that was not treated with antibiotics. He has no history of previous rheumatic fever. On examination his temperature is 38.6 degrees C.

His right ankle is swollen, warm, and tender. Cardiac auscultation reveals a grade 3 out of 6 pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. There is no rash, no subcutaneous nodules, and no involuntary movements.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 22, Temp 38.6 degrees C, BP 100/65 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right ankle swollen and tender, pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla, no chorea, no erythema marginatum, no subcutaneous nodules
data_table.Investigations: ASO titre 480 IU/mL (elevated), CRP 85 mg/L, ESR 65 mm/hr, WCC 13.2 x10^9/L. Echocardiogram: mild mitral regurgitation with mitral valve thickening. Throat swab: negative for group A streptococcus

lead_in: What is the most important management step after confirming the diagnosis?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin for 10 days to treat the pharyngitis
Commence IM benzathine penicillin G for secondary prophylaxis
Commence high-dose aspirin as primary treatment for this episode
Commence oral prednisolone for the carditis and joint symptoms
Observe and recheck the ASO titre in 4 weeks before treatment

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis vs transient synovitis - decision to aspirate
stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with a 1-day history of right hip pain and refusal to weight-bear. He had a mild upper respiratory tract infection 5 days ago that has since resolved. He has no significant past medical history and immunisations are up to date. On examination he is irritable and holds his right hip in flexion and external rotation.

He cries with any attempted passive range of motion of the right hip. There is no overlying erythema or swelling visible externally. His left hip has full painless range of motion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 24, Temp 38.5 degrees C, BP 95/60 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in flexion and external rotation, cries with passive movement, unable to weight-bear, no skin changes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 45 mg/L, ESR 32 mm/hr, blood cultures taken. Ultrasound right hip: moderate joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral antibiotics and arrange clinical review in 24 hours
Arrange MRI of the right hip before considering any intervention
Proceed to joint aspiration under ultrasound guidance promptly
Trial a course of NSAIDs with bed rest and reassess in 48 hours
Arrange a bone scan to exclude osteomyelitis before aspiration

subtopic_detail: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis - management urgency
stem:
A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of progressive left hip pain and an intermittent limp. He also reports left knee pain which prompted the initial presentation to his general practitioner 2 weeks ago. His GP prescribed paracetamol and advised rest. The pain has worsened and he now has difficulty walking. He is overweight with a BMI on the 95th centile.

He is Tanner stage 2 for pubic hair. On examination he has an antalgic gait. His left hip has limited internal rotation, and when the hip is flexed it obligatorily externally rotates. There is no effusion. Plain radiographs are obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 85, RR 18, Temp 36.7 degrees C, BP 115/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait, left hip limited internal rotation, obligatory external rotation with flexion, no effusion, BMI 95th centile
data_table.Investigations: AP pelvis X-ray: subtle widening of the left proximal femoral physis. Frog-leg lateral X-ray: posterior displacement of the left femoral epiphysis with a slip angle of approximately 35 degrees. Right hip: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence physiotherapy and a structured weight loss program
Arrange MRI of the left hip for further characterisation first
Prescribe analgesia and arrange orthopaedic review in two weeks
Make non-weight-bearing and arrange urgent orthopaedic pinning
Request bilateral hip CT scan for detailed surgical planning

subtopic_detail: Orbital cellulitis vs preseptal cellulitis - distinguishing features and management
stem:
A 5-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with progressive left periorbital swelling and redness over the past 2 days. She had been treated by her GP for acute sinusitis with oral amoxicillin for 5 days with minimal improvement. Over the past 12 hours her parents have noticed that her left eye appears to be bulging forward and she is complaining of pain when looking to the side.

She has had fevers to 39.2 degrees C. On examination there is marked left periorbital oedema and erythema. The left eye is proptotic with 3 mm of axial displacement. Extraocular movements are restricted in all directions with pain on attempted lateral gaze. Visual acuity is reduced in the left eye compared with the right. The right eye is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 125, RR 24, Temp 39.0 degrees C, BP 100/62 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Left periorbital oedema and erythema, 3 mm proptosis, restricted extraocular movements in all directions, pain with eye movement, reduced visual acuity left eye, right eye normal, no relative afferent pupillary defect
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.5 x10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, blood cultures taken. CT orbits with contrast: left medial subperiosteal abscess measuring 12 x 8 mm with adjacent ethmoid sinusitis, no intracranial extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and review as outpatient
Commence IV antibiotics alone and reassess at 48 hours for response
Prescribe topical chloramphenicol and oral antibiotics concurrently
Perform incision and drainage under local anaesthesia at bedside
Commence IV antibiotics and arrange urgent specialist surgical review

stem: A 14-year-old girl presents to the emergency department reporting that she took approximately 10 g of paracetamol in divided doses over an 8-hour period following an argument with her parents. She took the first dose at 6 pm and the last dose at 2 am. She presents at 4 am (10 hours after the first dose). She has no symptoms of nausea or vomiting. She takes no regular medications and has no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, abdomen soft and non-tender, no jaundice, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: ALT 22 U/L (ref <40), INR 1.0, creatinine 55 micromol/L, serum paracetamol 450 micromol/L at 10 hours post first ingestion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion immediately
Plot the paracetamol level on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram
Administer activated charcoal via nasogastric tube promptly
Send bloods and defer treatment pending ALT trend results
Observe with serial bloods for a further 8-hour period

subtopic_detail: Button battery lodged in oesophagus - urgency
stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who witnessed him swallow a coin-shaped object from a remote control approximately 2 hours ago. He has been drooling excessively and refusing to eat or drink since the ingestion. He has had one episode of non-bilious vomiting. He has no significant past medical history and is up to date with immunisations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, BP 90/55 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drooling, distressed, no stridor, no subcutaneous emphysema, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray shows a round radio-opaque foreign body at the level of the mid-oesophagus with a double-ring (halo) sign on anteroposterior view and step-off on lateral view

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Observe with repeat chest X-ray in 24 hours for passage
Arrange urgent endoscopic removal within 2 hours of ingestion
Administer oral honey every 10 minutes to reduce injury
Administer intravenous glucagon to promote distal passage
Attempt advancement into stomach using a nasogastric tube

stem: A 3-year-old girl (weight 14 kg) is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 2 hours after her mother found her with an open bottle of ferrous sulfate tablets. The mother estimates approximately 20 tablets (325 mg ferrous sulfate each, 65 mg elemental iron per tablet) may have been ingested, equating to approximately 93 mg/kg elemental iron. The child has vomited four times with blood-stained vomitus and is complaining of abdominal pain. She had one loose stool prior to arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150 bpm, BP 85/50 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 97% on room air, Temp 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, pale, tender abdomen diffusely, no peritonism, capillary refill 3 seconds peripherally
data_table.Investigations: Serum iron 95 micromol/L at 4 hours post-ingestion (ref 9-30), WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, glucose 12.5 mmol/L, venous pH 7.28, lactate 4.5 mmol/L, AXR shows multiple radio-opaque tablets in stomach and proximal small bowel

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal and observe with serial bloods
Arrange gastric lavage under general anaesthesia urgently
Commence IV deferoxamine infusion and whole bowel irrigation
Commence IV fluid resuscitation and supportive care alone
Administer oral desferrioxamine via nasogastric tube now

subtopic_detail: Skeletal survey findings concerning for NAI
stem: An 8-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because he has not been moving his left arm since this morning. The parents state he rolled off the change table onto carpet from a height of approximately 60 cm yesterday afternoon. He was born at term with no neonatal complications. He is formula-fed and growing along the 50th centile. There is no family history of bone disease. A skeletal survey has been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, BP 80/50 mmHg, RR 30, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Distressed when left arm is moved, swelling over mid-left humerus, no bruising on trunk, normal fontanelle, blue sclerae absent, teeth normal
data_table.Investigations: Left humerus X-ray: spiral fracture of the mid-shaft. Skeletal survey: healing posterior rib fractures of varying ages bilaterally (ribs 6-8 left, ribs 7-9 right), classic metaphyseal lesion (bucket-handle pattern) of the left distal tibia. FBC, UEC, calcium, phosphate, ALP, and vitamin D all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Accept the parental explanation and arrange outpatient review
Request bone density testing to exclude osteogenesis imperfecta
Obtain MRI of the left humerus for further characterisation
Notify child protection authorities and admit for assessment
Arrange genetic testing before involving child protection teams

subtopic_detail: Fabricated or induced illness - recognition and response
stem: A 6-year-old girl has been admitted to hospital 12 times over the past 2 years for reported generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Each episode is described in detail by her mother, who is a registered nurse. No seizure activity has ever been witnessed by hospital staff despite multiple admissions. The child is developmentally normal but has become increasingly anxious about medical procedures and hospital visits. Nursing staff have observed that reported events only occur when the mother is present at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 90 bpm, BP 100/60 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing child, neurologically intact, no focal deficits, anxious demeanour, multiple venepuncture scars on upper limbs
data_table.Investigations: EEG (x3): normal. MRI brain: normal. Serum prolactin post-reported events: within normal limits. All metabolic screening: normal. Full blood count and biochemistry: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial anticonvulsant medication to assess treatment response
Request prolonged inpatient video-EEG telemetry monitoring
Confront the mother directly with fabrication suspicions
Discharge home with outpatient neurology follow-up only
Convene a multidisciplinary strategy meeting with child protection

subtopic_detail: CMPA presenting as non-IgE mediated food protein-induced enterocolitis
stem: A 4-month-old boy who is exclusively breastfed is brought to his general practitioner with a 6-week history of chronic loose stools containing mucus and occasional blood streaks. He is irritable for 2-4 hours after feeds but settles between episodes. He has mild perioral eczema. His weight has tracked along the 40th centile since birth with no faltering. He was born at term via normal vaginal delivery and has no other medical history. His mother eats a regular diet including dairy products.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, RR 34, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C, weight 6.8 kg (40th centile)
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, mild perioral eczema, abdomen soft with active bowel sounds, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal perianal examination, nappy shows mucousy stool with small blood streak
data_table.Investigations: Skin prick test to cow's milk: negative (wheal 0 mm). Specific IgE to cow's milk: less than 0.10 kU/L. FBC: mild eosinophilia (eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence maternal cow's milk protein elimination for 2-4 weeks
Switch from breastfeeding to a soy-based infant formula immediately
Commence an extensively hydrolysed formula and cease breastfeeds
Trial a proton pump inhibitor as initial empiric therapy
Arrange upper and lower endoscopy with mucosal biopsy samples

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis action plan - adrenaline device prescription
stem:
A 5-year-old boy (weighing 22 kg) is recovering in the emergency department following an episode of anaphylaxis after eating a biscuit containing peanut at a birthday party. He developed generalised urticaria, then vomiting, audible wheeze, and became pale and floppy. Paramedics administered intramuscular adrenaline 150 mcg and he responded well. In the emergency department, he received a further dose of intramuscular adrenaline 150 mcg for recurrent wheeze 20 minutes later.

He has been stable for 4 hours with no further symptoms. Specific IgE to peanut returns at 28 kU/L. He has a background of mild eczema but no prior allergic reactions to foods.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100 bpm, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, chest clear, no urticaria, no angioedema, well perfused peripherally
data_table.Investigations: Serum tryptase (drawn at 1 hour): 18 mcg/L (ref <11.5). Specific IgE peanut: 28 kU/L (strongly positive). FBC and UEC: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan for this patient?

options.text: Prescribe adrenaline autoinjector 300 mcg (EpiPen) with ASCIA Action Plan, training, and allergist referral
Prescribe adrenaline autoinjector 150 mcg (EpiPen Jr) with ASCIA Action Plan, training, and allergist referral
Prescribe oral cetirizine and a salbutamol inhaler for any future acute allergic events while awaiting allergist input
Arrange supervised peanut oral immunotherapy desensitisation before discharge from the emergency department this evening
Prescribe a 3-day oral prednisolone course and arrange GP review without an adrenaline autoinjector at discharge today

stem: A 9-month-old girl is brought to the general practitioner by her mother who has noticed a white glow in her daughter's left eye in photographs taken over the past 2 months. The child is otherwise well, feeding normally, and reaching developmental milestones. She was born at 38 weeks gestation with no neonatal complications. There is no family history of eye cancer or genetic conditions. On examination, the red reflex is absent in the left eye and present in the right eye. Visual tracking appears normal bilaterally.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, RR 30, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C, weight 8.5 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing infant, anterior segments of both eyes appear normal, left pupil shows white reflex on direct ophthalmoscopy, right red reflex present and normal, no proptosis, no periorbital swelling
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed prior to presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange routine ophthalmology outpatient review within 4 weeks
Commence empiric topical chloramphenicol for possible infection
Arrange urgent ophthalmology examination under anaesthesia and MRI
Reassure and repeat the red reflex test at the 12-month health check
Request CT orbit with contrast as the first-line imaging study

subtopic_detail: Posterior fossa tumour presenting with raised intracranial pressure
stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of progressively worsening early morning headaches associated with vomiting. Over the past 5 days he has developed an unsteady gait and his parents report he has been bumping into objects. He has no significant past medical history. His immunisations are up to date. There is no family history of neurological conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 68 bpm, BP 130/85 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy, bilateral sixth nerve palsies, truncal ataxia with broad-based gait, past-pointing on finger-nose testing, no limb weakness, no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain with gadolinium: 4 cm heterogeneously enhancing midline posterior fossa mass arising from the fourth ventricle with associated obstructive hydrocephalus, no evidence of leptomeningeal dissemination on cranio-spinal imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence IV dexamethasone and arrange serial lumbar punctures
Arrange stereotactic biopsy of the lesion as the initial step
Start empiric combination chemotherapy before pursuing surgery
Arrange urgent neurosurgical referral for CSF diversion and resection
Commence IV mannitol infusion and arrange transfer to rehabilitation

subtopic_detail: Paediatric sepsis - fluid resuscitation and reassessment
stem: A 2-year-old girl (weight 12 kg) is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with a 12-hour history of fever, poor oral intake, and increasing lethargy. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 3 days ago. On arrival, she is drowsy but rousable, with mottled peripheries. Intravenous access has been established and she has received one 20 mL/kg (240 mL) bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 10 minutes. Broad-spectrum antibiotics have been administered. Following the first bolus, she remains tachycardic and hypotensive with mottled skin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 175 bpm, BP 60/35 mmHg (below 5th centile for age), RR 42, SpO2 94% on high-flow oxygen, Temp 39.8 degrees C, CRT 5 seconds centrally
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, mottled peripheries, cool extremities, no rash, no meningism, tachypnoeic with no added sounds, abdomen soft, fontanelle closed
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.5 x10^9/L, neutrophils 18.2 x10^9/L, Hb 112 g/L, platelets 145 x10^9/L, CRP 185 mg/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L, Na 136 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 45 micromol/L, venous pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L, BE -12

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to 4% albumin solution for the second fluid bolus dose
Commence a dopamine infusion via the peripheral intravenous line
Administer a rapid 40 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 5 minutes now
Reduce fluid rate to maintenance and commence standard IV fluids
Give a second 20 mL/kg bolus and prepare inotropes if no response

stem: A 15-year-old girl is referred by her GP with a 6-month history of progressively restrictive eating and excessive exercise. Her parents report she has lost approximately 25% of her pre-morbid weight. She denies any problems and is reluctant to engage. She has not had a menstrual period for 4 months.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 42 bpm (overnight), BP 88/52 mmHg supine with postural drop 25 mmHg on standing, T 35.2 C, RR 14
data_table.Examination: BMI 15.2 kg/m2, lanugo hair on arms and back, dry skin with peripheral cyanosis, muscle wasting, parotid enlargement absent
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus bradycardia, QTc 480 ms. Na 136 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L, phosphate 0.72 mmol/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, Hb 118 g/L, WCC 3.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for medical stabilisation with cardiac monitoring and supervised refeeding
Refer to outpatient dietitian for weekly weigh-ins and structured meal planning
Commence fluoxetine for comorbid depression and arrange review in two weeks
Enrol in an eating disorder day program with family-based therapy sessions
Arrange psychiatric admission for compulsory treatment under the Mental Health Act

subtopic_detail: ADHD medication initiation in adolescent - first-line choice
stem: A 14-year-old boy is reviewed in clinic following a comprehensive ADHD assessment. Conners parent and teacher rating scales are consistent with ADHD-combined type. School reports document declining academic performance and behavioural difficulties. He has completed a structured behavioural management program over 6 months with limited effect on symptoms. He has no cardiac history, no family history of sudden death, and no history of substance use.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, weight 55 kg, height 168 cm
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular examination, no murmurs, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: ECG: normal sinus rhythm, QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence atomoxetine 40 mg daily as the preferred first-line agent
Commence methylphenidate immediate-release at low dose with titration
Commence dexamfetamine extended-release capsules as initial treatment
Trial omega-3 fatty acid supplementation before considering stimulants
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy as sole ongoing management

stem: A 3-year-old girl with moderate atopic eczema managed with regular emollients and mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment is brought to the emergency department. Over 2 days she has developed widespread clustered vesicles and punched-out erosions over her face, neck, and upper chest. She is febrile, irritable, and refusing to eat. There is no history of contact with anyone with cold sores, though she attends day care.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 145 bpm, T 39.2 C, RR 28, BP 90/55 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Clustered monomorphic vesicles and shallow punched-out erosions on face, neck, and upper chest, some with haemorrhagic crusting, periorbital oedema bilaterally, no corneal involvement on fluorescein examination
data_table.Investigations: Tzanck smear: multinucleated giant cells identified. FBC: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, Hb 112 g/L, platelets 280 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase topical corticosteroid potency and add emollient wraps
Commence oral flucloxacillin for secondary bacterial skin infection
Commence IV aciclovir and withhold topical corticosteroids
Apply topical mupirocin ointment to erosions three times daily
Commence oral valaciclovir and continue topical corticosteroids

subtopic_detail: Immune thrombocytopenia - management based on bleeding and count
stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who noticed widespread bruising and small red spots on his legs and trunk over the past week. He has been otherwise well with no recent fevers, weight loss, bone pain, or lymphadenopathy. He had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 3 weeks ago. He is active and playful in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100 bpm, T 36.8 C, BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae on lower limbs and trunk, scattered bruising on shins and arms, no mucosal bleeding, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, well-appearing child
data_table.Investigations: Platelet count 8 x10^9/L, Hb 128 g/L, WCC 7.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 3.8 x10^9/L, blood film: isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets, no blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for a four-day course
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as a single infusion
Arrange urgent bone marrow aspirate to exclude acute leukaemia
Observe with restricted activity and outpatient follow-up within 48 hours
Commence tranexamic acid and arrange urgent platelet transfusion

subtopic_detail: Major paediatric burns - fluid resuscitation calculation
stem: A 7-year-old boy (25 kg) is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove 1 hour ago. He has sustained scald burns to his anterior torso and both upper limbs. Using the Lund and Browder chart, the total body surface area burned is estimated at 25%. The burns are mixed superficial and deep partial thickness. He is alert, crying, and in significant pain. IV access has been obtained in an unburned limb.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, BP 100/65 mmHg, T 36.0 C, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air, CRT 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Erythematous and blistered areas across anterior chest, abdomen, and bilateral upper limbs, skin moist with intact sensation, no circumferential burns, airway patent with no soot or facial burns
data_table.Investigations: Weight 25 kg, urine output not yet measured, Hb 135 g/L, Na 139 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, glucose 7.2 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid resuscitation strategy?

options.text: Administer 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus then commence standard maintenance
Commence colloid resuscitation with 4% albumin infusion over 4 hours
Apply silver sulfadiazine dressings and encourage oral fluid intake only
Commence half-normal saline at double the standard maintenance fluid rate
Commence Parkland formula fluids with urinary catheter output monitoring

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with acute wheeze and dyspnoea worsening over 4 hours. He has moderate persistent asthma and uses fluticasone propionate 125 mcg twice daily. He took 6 puffs of salbutamol via spacer at home without relief. On arrival he received oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. Over the past hour he has received 3 nebulised salbutamol doses at 20-minute intervals with minimal improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142 bpm, RR 36/min, SpO2 91% on 8 L/min face mask O2, temperature 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Unable to speak in full sentences, widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry at bases, moderate intercostal recession, using accessory muscles
data_table.Investigations: No chest X-ray performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next addition to management?

options.text: Administer a repeat dose of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg now
Request an urgent portable chest X-ray before further therapy
Commence continuous nebulised salbutamol infusion at 10 mg/h
Add nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 mcg to the next salbutamol
Prepare intravenous salbutamol loading dose followed by infusion

stem: A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department at 11 pm with a 12-hour history of barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarse voice preceded by 2 days of rhinorrhoea. She received oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg from the triage nurse 30 minutes ago. She continues to have stridor at rest with moderate recession and is becoming increasingly distressed with handling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, RR 32/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate subcostal and sternal recession, alert, sitting upright on mother's lap, no drooling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer a second dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg now to augment the airway anti-inflammatory effect
Request an urgent lateral soft tissue neck X-ray for assessment of subglottic narrowing in this distressed child
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 as a flat dose with oxygen, with at least 3 hours of post-adrenaline observation per RCH
Arrange urgent ENT referral for fibreoptic nasopharyngoscopy to exclude a foreign body or epiglottic pathology
Commence humidified oxygen via face mask and reassess in 1 hour after waiting for the dexamethasone to take full effect

subtopic_detail: SVT in infant: vagal failure escalation
stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department by his parents who noticed pallor, irritability, and poor feeding over the past 6 hours. He was born at term with no prior medical history. An ECG shows narrow complex tachycardia at 280 bpm with no discernible P waves. Two attempts at ice-water slurry applied to the face for 15 seconds each have been unsuccessful.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 280 bpm, RR 55/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: Pale, capillary refill time 3 seconds centrally, 2 cm hepatomegaly below costal margin, femoral pulses palpable bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone 5 mg/kg over 30 minutes
Perform synchronised DC cardioversion starting at 1 J/kg
Administer a loading dose of intravenous digoxin at 10 mcg/kg
Commence intravenous flecainide infusion at 2 mg/kg over 20 min
Administer rapid intravenous adenosine 100 mcg/kg via proximal vein

stem: A 3-day-old term neonate is noted to have a grade 3/6 harsh pansystolic murmur loudest at the left lower sternal border during routine postnatal examination. He is feeding well and there is no cyanosis. His older sibling was diagnosed with an atrial septal defect at age 4 years. The 4-limb blood pressure readings are normal and pre-ductal and post-ductal saturations are 99% and 98% respectively.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 145 bpm, RR 44/min, SpO2 pre-ductal 99% / post-ductal 98%, temperature 36.8 C, weight 3.4 kg
data_table.Examination: Active, pink, well-perfused, normal femoral pulses, no hepatomegaly, grade 3/6 harsh pansystolic murmur LLSE with thrill

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography within 24 to 48 hours
Reassurance and outpatient paediatric review at 6 weeks
Chest X-ray and 12-lead ECG before deciding on echocardiography
Commence oral prostaglandin E1 and transfer to a cardiac centre
Arrange cardiac CT angiography for detailed anatomical assessment

stem: A 10-year-old girl with no prior medical history presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of polyuria, polydipsia, and vomiting. Her parents report she has lost 3 kg over the past 2 weeks. She is drowsy but rousable and has deep, rapid breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 bpm, RR 34/min (Kussmaul pattern), SpO2 99% on room air, BP 95/60 mmHg, temperature 36.5 C, weight 32 kg
data_table.Investigations: BGL 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.08, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, Na 131 mmol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L, urea 8.2 mmol/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, corrected Na 137 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid management strategy?

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9% normal saline bolus followed by rapid rehydration over 12 hours
10 mL/kg 0.9% normal saline bolus then deficit replacement over 48 hours
Commence insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h before any fluid administration
20 mL/kg 0.9% normal saline bolus repeated twice then rehydrate over 48 hours
Commence 0.45% half-normal saline with 5% dextrose from the outset of therapy

stem: A 2-day-old term male neonate, birth weight 4.6 kg, was born to a mother without gestational diabetes. He has had 3 documented episodes of blood glucose below 2.0 mmol/L despite 4-hourly breastfeeds supplemented with formula top-ups. He required a 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose bolus for a glucose of 1.4 mmol/L 6 hours ago and is now on a dextrose infusion at 8 mg/kg/min. His glucose has just dropped to 1.8 mmol/L on the current infusion rate.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, RR 42/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Large for gestational age, no dysmorphic features, no hepatomegaly, jittery when handled
data_table.Investigations: BGL 1.8 mmol/L on dextrose infusion 8 mg/kg/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate set of investigations to collect at the time of the next hypoglycaemic episode?

options.text: Serum cortisol and thyroid function tests with urine metabolic screen
Repeat blood glucose with simultaneous serum lactate and blood gas only
Cranial ultrasound and anterior pituitary hormone panel including GH
Critical sample: insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, GH, FFA, ketones, and lactate
Urine organic acids, plasma amino acids, and acylcarnitine profile

stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred for short stature. Her height is 108 cm (well below the 3rd percentile; mid-parental height target is 25th percentile). Growth velocity over the past year was 3.5 cm/year. She has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, low posterior hairline, and bilateral cubitus valgus. She has no hearing difficulties. Her karyotype confirms 45,X.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 98/62 mmHg, height 108 cm (below 3rd percentile), weight 22 kg (10th percentile)
data_table.Investigations: Karyotype: 45,X. TSH 3.2 mIU/L (normal), free T4 14 pmol/L (normal), coeliac serology negative, IGF-1 low-normal for age, renal ultrasound normal, echocardiography shows bicuspid aortic valve without stenosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding her growth?

options.text: Reassure the family and recheck growth velocity in 12 months
Commence low-dose oestradiol to induce puberty and promote growth
Refer to paediatric endocrinology for growth hormone therapy initiation
Request growth hormone stimulation testing before any treatment decision
Commence oxandrolone as an alternative to promote linear growth

stem: A 5-year-old boy with known peanut allergy accidentally ingests a biscuit containing peanut at a school event. Within 10 minutes he develops generalised urticaria, facial swelling, and audible wheeze. His teacher administered his prescribed adrenaline autoinjector (150 mcg) into his lateral thigh 5 minutes ago. He arrives in the emergency department by ambulance.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150 bpm, RR 32/min, SpO2 92% on room air, BP 80/50 mmHg, temperature 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, periorbital and lip swelling, widespread wheeze bilaterally, capillary refill time 3 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intramuscular adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (1:1000) into the lateral thigh
Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as the priority medication
Commence nebulised salbutamol 5 mg and reassess before further adrenaline
Administer intravenous adrenaline 10 mcg/kg as a slow push over 5 minutes
Administer oral cetirizine 10 mg and observe for clinical improvement

stem: A 4-month-old exclusively formula-fed infant presents with a 6-week history of blood-streaked loose stools, irritability after feeds, and poor weight gain. She was switched from standard cow's milk-based formula to a soy-based formula 2 weeks ago with no improvement. There is no fever, no vomiting, and no family history of coeliac disease. Examination reveals perianal erythema but is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, RR 36/min, temperature 37.1 C, weight 5.2 kg (dropped from 25th to 10th percentile)
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 105 g/L, WCC 9.2 x10^9/L, eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L (mildly elevated), platelets 340 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in feeding management?

options.text: Refer for endoscopy and colonic biopsy before changing formula
Commence a hydrolysed rice-based formula and review in 2 to 4 weeks
Return to standard cow's milk formula as soy failure excludes CMPA
Trial goat's milk formula as an alternative protein source
Switch to an extensively hydrolysed formula and review in 2 to 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Atopic eczema flare: wet dressing therapy
stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a severe flare of atopic eczema affecting 40% body surface area. She has been using regular emollients and intermittent methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% cream for the past 6 months. Her current flare has not responded to 2 weeks of twice-daily topical corticosteroid application. There is no clinical evidence of secondary bacterial infection. She is scratching constantly and sleeping poorly.

data_table.Examination: Widespread erythematous, excoriated, lichenified plaques on flexural surfaces, trunk, and limbs affecting approximately 40% BSA, no weeping, no crusting, no pustules, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Skin swab: no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a 5-day course of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily
Initiate wet dressing therapy with diluted topical corticosteroid
Switch to tacrolimus 0.03% ointment twice daily to all areas
Commence oral azathioprine 2 mg/kg daily as steroid-sparing agent
Add oral flucloxacillin for 7 days to cover subclinical infection

stem: A 3-year-old boy is referred by his GP for poor weight gain and intermittent loose, pale stools over 6 months. He was weaned onto wheat-containing solids at 6 months. His 8-year-old sister was diagnosed with coeliac disease last year. He has been on a normal gluten-containing diet.

data_table.Vital signs: Weight 12 kg (below 3rd percentile, previously 25th), height 92 cm (10th percentile)
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) 148 U/mL (normal below 7), total IgA 0.6 g/L (normal for age), Hb 102 g/L, ferritin 8 mcg/L, folate low at 5.2 nmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Commence a gluten-free diet immediately and recheck tTG-IgA in 6 months
Confirm with endomysial antibody (EMA) IgA testing and HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing
Refer for upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy while on gluten
Request HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping as the sole confirmatory test
Repeat the tTG-IgA test in 3 months to confirm sustained elevation

subtopic_detail: Bacterial meningitis: empiric antibiotics by age
stem: A 5-week-old infant presents to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of fever, poor feeding, and irritability. He was born at term with no neonatal complications. His fontanelle is full and tense. He has received his birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180 bpm, RR 52/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.9 C (rectal), CRT 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Irritable, high-pitched cry, full and tense anterior fontanelle, no rash, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 320 x10^6/L (90% polymorphs), protein 2.1 g/L, glucose 0.8 mmol/L (paired serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L), Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily as monotherapy with no additional antibiotic added at this stage of the workup
Intravenous benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) plus gentamicin plus cefotaxime, all at meningitic doses, as the Australian regimen for this presentation
Intravenous vancomycin plus meropenem at meningitic doses as broad cover for resistant pathogens in this previously well neonate
Intravenous cefotaxime plus ampicillin at meningitic doses without the addition of gentamicin, as per the US AAP febrile-infant pathway
Intravenous flucloxacillin plus cefotaxime at meningitic doses to cover Staphylococcus aureus and Gram-negative pathogens in this very young neonate

stem: A 6-month-old girl presents with fever of 38.8 C for 2 days, irritability and reduced wet nappies. She has no prior urinary tract infection. A catheter urine specimen confirms a urinary tract infection with pure growth of E. coli. She responds well to oral cefalexin and is afebrile within 48 hours with no atypical features. Her antenatal anomaly scans were complete and normal, and there is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux. This is her first documented urinary tract infection.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, RR 34/min, temperature 38.8 C, weight 7.5 kg
data_table.Investigations: Urine MCS: E. coli >10^8 CFU/L (pure growth), sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanate; FBC and CRP consistent with bacterial infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation following treatment?

options.text: No routine imaging is required after this typical first urinary tract infection; counsel the family on prompt urine testing with any future fever
Renal tract ultrasound within 2 weeks of the acute infection as routine post-urinary-tract-infection imaging in any infant under 6 months of age
Micturating cystourethrogram as the first-line imaging investigation to exclude vesicoureteric reflux after this first urinary tract infection
DMSA renal cortical scan performed at 6 months after the infection to detect cortical scarring before any further febrile illness develops
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast to exclude renal abscess and complex anatomical anomaly in this young infant patient

stem: A 14-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes at home. His mother reports he had a runny nose for 2 days and she noticed a temperature of 39.2 C just before the seizure. He has no prior seizure history and his development is normal. He is now alert, interactive, and feeding well. There is no rash and no neck stiffness. His fontanelle is flat and soft.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120 bpm, RR 28/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 C (axillary), GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful, non-toxic appearing, bilateral clear rhinorrhoea, bilateral TMs erythematous, no neck stiffness, no bulging fontanelle, normal tone and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis before discharge
Admit for 24-hour observation with continuous EEG monitoring
Commence prophylactic sodium valproate to prevent recurrence
Request urgent CT brain to exclude structural intracranial pathology
Provide parent education on seizure first aid and safe discharge

stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with a 3-day history of spontaneous bruising and petechiae over her trunk and limbs. She had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago. She is otherwise well with no bleeding from mucous membranes, no haematuria, and no neurological symptoms. She has no hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 95 bpm, RR 22/min, temperature 36.8 C, BP 95/60 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 125 g/L, WCC 7.8 x10^9/L (normal differential), platelets 8 x10^9/L. Blood film: reduced platelets, large platelets seen, no blasts, no fragmented red cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for 5 to 7 days
Observation with activity restriction and serial platelet counts
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as a single dose
Request urgent bone marrow aspirate to exclude leukaemia
Commence oral eltrombopag 25 mg daily as a thrombopoietin agonist

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with acute onset of limping and refusal to weight-bear on his right leg since this morning. He had a mild upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago. He appears unwell and is lying still on the bed. His right hip is held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation. He screams with any attempt at passive hip movement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, RR 24/min, temperature 39.1 C, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in flexion and external rotation, marked limitation and pain with passive range of motion especially internal rotation, no skin rash, no joint swelling of knee or ankle
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, CRP 85 mg/L, ESR 55 mm/h, blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral ibuprofen and outpatient orthopaedic review in 48 hours
Commence IV antibiotics and observe for clinical improvement
Urgent hip ultrasound followed by joint aspiration if effusion present
Plain X-ray of the right hip and pelvis as the initial investigation
MRI of the right hip with gadolinium to characterise the pathology

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother 90 minutes after being found with an open bottle of children's paracetamol. The bottle previously contained approximately 200 mL of suspension (24 mg/mL). Based on the remaining volume, the estimated ingestion is approximately 180 mg/kg. She is currently asymptomatic and has no vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 C, weight 14 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful, non-tender abdomen, no jaundice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg and draw paracetamol level at 4 hours
Induce emesis with ipecac syrup to reduce the absorbed dose
Obtain liver function tests and reassess if abnormal in 12 hours
Commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine and draw a 4-hour level
Observe for 4 hours and treat only if the level is above the line

stem: A 5-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department by his father with a swollen left thigh noticed during a nappy change. The father states the infant rolled off the change table 2 days ago but seemed fine afterwards. The infant is non-ambulatory. On examination you note the left thigh is swollen and tender. You also observe several circular bruises of varying ages on his trunk.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 145 bpm, RR 36/min, temperature 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: Left thigh swollen, tender, and shortened with external rotation; multiple circular bruises (0.5 to 1.5 cm diameter) on anterior chest and back in various stages of healing; frenulum intact, no retinal haemorrhages on fundoscopy
data_table.Investigations: X-ray left femur: spiral fracture of the mid-shaft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?

options.text: Accept the mechanism and refer to orthopaedics for fracture management
Notify child protection services and arrange a skeletal survey
Request coagulation studies and discharge if results are normal
Discuss concerns with the father and allow voluntary re-presentation
Arrange CT head and full-body MRI as the primary imaging protocol

stem: A 21-day-old term female neonate presents to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.3 C measured rectally at home. She was born via normal vaginal delivery with no maternal risk factors for sepsis. She has been feeding adequately and has no rash. Her mother reports she has been slightly more sleepy than usual over the past 12 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170 bpm, RR 48/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.5 C (rectal), CRT 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mildly lethargic but rousable, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no rash, no hepatosplenomegaly, mild tachypnoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Obtain blood and urine cultures, commence IV ampicillin and gentamicin
Obtain blood cultures only and observe for 6 hours before antibiotics
Administer oral amoxicillin and arrange next-day GP follow-up
Obtain blood cultures and commence IV ceftriaxone as monotherapy
Check a urine dipstick and treat only if positive for nitrites

stem: A 10-week-old infant born at 32 weeks gestation (corrected age 2 weeks) presents in July with 2 days of coryza and increasing feeding difficulty. She was discharged from the neonatal unit at 36 weeks corrected without home oxygen. She did not receive palivizumab. Her mother reports she managed only half her usual breast milk volume at the last 2 feeds and has had one brief apnoea witnessed at home.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165 bpm, RR 62/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 37.5 C, weight 3.1 kg
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, fine crackles right base, nasal flaring intermittently, alert between handling
data_table.Investigations: NPA: RSV positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate level of care for this infant?

options.text: Discharge home with parental education and next-day GP follow-up
Admit to a general paediatric ward for standard monitoring
Commence HFNC at 2 L/kg/min and admit to a monitored area
Administer IM palivizumab and observe for 4 hours before deciding
Admit to a high-dependency area with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring

stem: A 3-day-old term male neonate (birth weight 3.5 kg, gestational age 39 weeks) is noted to be jaundiced on the postnatal ward. He was born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. He is breastfeeding well with 8 to 10 feeds per day and has passed meconium. His mother's blood group is O positive with no atypical antibodies. The baby's blood group is A positive with a positive direct Coombs test.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, RR 38/min, temperature 37.0 C, weight 3.35 kg (4% loss from birth weight)
data_table.Investigations: Transcutaneous bilirubin 290 micromol/L at 60 hours of age, Hb 165 g/L, reticulocyte count 8%, blood group A positive, DAT positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and recheck bilirubin in 24 hours
Supplement with formula feeds and recheck bilirubin in 6 hours
Commence intensive phototherapy and recheck bilirubin in 6 hours
Arrange immediate exchange transfusion via umbilical venous catheter
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as haemolysis treatment

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease: IVIG timing and aspirin regimen
stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with 6 days of persistent high fever (above 39 C) unresponsive to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips, a polymorphous truncal rash, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy measuring 2 cm. His hands and feet are oedematous and erythematous. He is irritable but haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, RR 28/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.5 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.5 x10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, Hb 108 g/L, platelets 380 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 65 U/L, Na 132 mmol/L, sterile pyuria on urine microscopy, echocardiogram: no coronary artery abnormalities at baseline

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: High-dose oral aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in divided doses alone
Intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg for 3 consecutive days
Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone pending blood culture results
IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus high-dose aspirin concurrently
Defer treatment until repeat echocardiogram at day 10 of illness

stem: A 12-day-old male neonate, born at term with a birth weight of 3.4 kg, presents to the emergency department with poor feeding, lethargy, and vomiting for 2 days. He has lost 15% of his birth weight. His newborn screening card was collected on day 3 but results have not yet returned. The referring GP notes the genitalia appear normal. He was well at birth and in the first week of life.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 180 bpm, RR 56/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.2 C, CRT 4 seconds, weight 2.89 kg
data_table.Examination: Severely dehydrated, mottled, lethargic but rousable, sunken fontanelle, normal male genitalia with bilateral descended testes, no hyperpigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Na 118 mmol/L, K 8.2 mmol/L, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, venous pH 7.18, HCO3 10 mmol/L, ECG shows peaked T waves and widened QRS

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis and appropriate targeted treatment?

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia - IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat and fluid resuscitation
Pyloric stenosis - IV saline resuscitation and urgent surgical pyloromyotomy
Galactosaemia - withdraw lactose feeds and commence soy-based formula
Congenital renal tubular acidosis - IV sodium bicarbonate infusion
Sepsis with adrenal haemorrhage - IV ceftriaxone and vasopressor support

stem: A 10-month-old girl presents with 7 days of fever above 39 C. She has non-purulent bilateral conjunctival injection and cracked red lips but no rash, no extremity changes, and no lymphadenopathy. She has been irritable with a poor appetite. Two courses of oral amoxicillin prescribed by her GP have not reduced the fever. Her GP is uncertain about the diagnosis because she does not meet full Kawasaki disease criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150 bpm, RR 30/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.3 C
data_table.Investigations: CRP 95 mg/L, ESR 65 mm/h, WCC 22 x10^9/L, Hb 98 g/L, platelets 520 x10^9/L, albumin 25 g/L, ALT 72 U/L, urine microscopy: sterile pyuria (50 WBC per HPF, culture negative), echocardiogram: left coronary artery z-score 2.8 (mildly dilated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue observation and repeat echocardiogram in 1 week
Arrange urgent cardiac catheterisation for coronary assessment
Commence oral prednisolone and low-dose aspirin as outpatient
Treat as viral illness and review if fever persists beyond day 10
Commence IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin for incomplete Kawasaki disease

subtopic_detail: ADEM versus first episode MS: diagnostic discrimination
stem: An 8-year-old girl presents with a 3-day progressive history of ataxia, right-sided weakness, and new-onset urinary incontinence. Two weeks ago she had a febrile illness with pharyngitis. She has no prior neurological history. Her MRI brain shows large, bilateral, poorly demarcated T2 hyperintense lesions in the deep white matter, thalami, and basal ganglia with patchy gadolinium enhancement. Her MRI spine shows a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis lesion spanning T4 to T8. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein but negative oligoclonal bands.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, RR 18/min, temperature 37.8 C, BP 100/62 mmHg, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Examination: Ataxic gait, right hemiparesis (power 3/5), hyperreflexia bilaterally, bilateral upgoing plantars, urinary retention with palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: large bilateral deep white matter, thalamic, and basal ganglia T2 lesions with patchy enhancement. MRI spine: LETM T4-T8. CSF: WCC 45 x10^6/L (lymphocytic), protein 0.82 g/L, glucose normal, OCB negative, MOG antibody positive in serum

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: CNS lymphoma - urgent neurosurgical biopsy and oncology referral
ADEM - IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 5 days
Paediatric MS - IV methylprednisolone then commence fingolimod
Neuromyelitis optica - IV methylprednisolone then rituximab
HSV encephalitis - urgent IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, pallor, and easy bruising. He has painless bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. His peripheral blood smear shows blast cells. A bone marrow aspirate confirms pre-B cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with a white cell count of 180 x10^9/L. He is about to commence induction chemotherapy. His baseline renal function and electrolytes are currently normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, RR 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 180 x10^9/L (85% blasts), Hb 72 g/L, platelets 28 x10^9/L, Na 140 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, urea 4.5 mmol/L, creatinine 45 micromol/L, uric acid 0.52 mmol/L (mildly elevated), phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, calcium 2.35 mmol/L, LDH 2800 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic strategy for tumour lysis syndrome before starting chemotherapy?

options.text: Oral allopurinol 10 mg/kg/day and standard maintenance IV fluids
Intravenous rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg, aggressive IV hydration, and monitoring
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine and prevent crystals
Oral allopurinol plus oral phosphate binder and fluid restriction
Defer chemotherapy until uric acid normalises with hydration alone

stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a sudden choking episode while eating peanuts 2 hours ago.
