His parents performed back blows at the scene and the choking resolved, but he has had a persistent cough since. He has no prior respiratory history and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 34, SpO2 95% on room air, Temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession. Right-sided wheeze on auscultation with decreased air entry at the right base. Left lung clear. No stridor at rest.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: hyperinflation of the right lung with mediastinal shift to the left on expiratory film. No radio-opaque foreign body seen.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Chest physiotherapy and observation for 24 hours
Flexible nasendoscopy under local anaesthesia
CT chest with three-dimensional reconstruction
Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
Oral dexamethasone and reassessment in 4 hours

subtopic_detail: Chronic suppurative otitis media in Aboriginal child
stem: A 6-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote Northern Territory community presents to the visiting ear health clinic. His mother reports persistent discharge from his right ear for the past 5 months. He has had three courses of oral amoxicillin over this period with no improvement. His school teacher has raised concerns about inattention in class. He is otherwise well with no fever or systemic symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Right ear: mucopurulent discharge through a large central tympanic membrane perforation. Left ear: dull tympanic membrane with mild retraction. No mastoid tenderness bilaterally. No facial nerve palsy.
data_table.Investigations: Pure tone audiometry: 35 dB conductive hearing loss right ear, 20 dB conductive hearing loss left ear.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for a further 14 days
Topical ciprofloxacin drops with regular aural toilet
Urgent referral for tympanoplasty and mastoidectomy
Intravenous ceftriaxone daily for 7 days in hospital
Grommet insertion under general anaesthesia bilaterally

subtopic_detail: Retropharyngeal abscess - deep neck space infection
stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a 3-day history of fever, progressive neck stiffness, and refusal to eat. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago that appeared to resolve. Over the past 24 hours she has developed drooling and a muffled voice. She holds her neck in extension and resists flexion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, RR 30, SpO2 97% on room air, Temp 39.4 C
data_table.Examination: Toxic-appearing child. Neck held in slight extension. Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy bilaterally. Oropharynx: midline posterior pharyngeal wall bulge visible. No trismus.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 18.1), CRP 145 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV flucloxacillin and metronidazole with urgent CT neck
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and outpatient follow-up
Lateral neck X-ray and IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy
Direct laryngoscopy and immediate incision and drainage
IV dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline with observation

subtopic_detail: Primary nocturnal enuresis - management after alarm failure
stem: A 9-year-old boy presents with ongoing primary nocturnal enuresis. He wets the bed 5 nights per week and has never had a sustained dry period. He has no daytime symptoms, no constipation, and no urinary tract infections. A 3-month trial of an enuresis alarm was attempted with good compliance but produced no improvement. His urinalysis is normal and postvoid residual is negligible on ultrasound.

data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.020, no protein, no glucose, no leucocytes, no nitrites. Renal tract ultrasound: normal kidneys and bladder, postvoid residual < 10 mL.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat the enuresis alarm trial for a further 3 months
Fluid restriction after 5pm with scheduled overnight waking
Oral desmopressin melt at bedtime for an initial 3-month trial
Oral oxybutynin for overactive bladder with enuresis component
Referral for urodynamic studies and specialist urology review

stem: A 15-year-old boy is referred by his GP for absent pubertal development. He has no pubic hair, testicular volumes are 2 mL bilaterally, and he has not had a growth spurt. He is at the 3rd centile for height. His father reports that he himself was a late developer who did not shave until age 18. The boy is otherwise well with no chronic illness, headaches, or visual disturbance. He has a normal sense of smell.

data_table.Vital signs: Height 152 cm (3rd centile), weight 43 kg (10th centile), BMI 18.6
data_table.Investigations: LH 1.2 IU/L, FSH 1.8 IU/L, testosterone 0.8 nmol/L, prolactin 180 mIU/L (normal), IGF-1 low-normal for age, bone age 12.5 years (chronological age 15 years)

lead_in: What is the single most useful investigation to distinguish constitutional delay from hypogonadotropic hypogonadism?

options.text: Karyotype analysis for chromosomal abnormalities
GnRH stimulation test with serial LH measurements
Serum inhibin B and anti-Mullerian hormone levels
Serum kisspeptin and neurokinin B measurement
MRI brain with pituitary protocol and olfactory assessment

subtopic_detail: Acute scrotal pain - testicular torsion exploration
stem: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with sudden onset severe left scrotal pain that began 3 hours ago during a basketball game. He has vomited twice and the pain radiates to the left groin. He denies urinary symptoms, penile discharge, or recent trauma. He has no prior episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 125/75 mmHg, Temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Left testis high-riding and transversely oriented. Absent cremasteric reflex on the left. Exquisitely tender left hemiscrotum with a firm, swollen testis. Right testis normal. No erythema of scrotal skin. Negative Prehn sign.
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: no leucocytes, no nitrites, no blood.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Urgent scrotal Doppler ultrasound to confirm diagnosis
Immediate surgical exploration and orchidopexy
Manual detorsion attempt with analgesia in the ED
IV antibiotics for presumed epididymo-orchitis
Analgesia and repeat examination in 2 hours

subtopic_detail: Appendicitis in young child - atypical presentation
stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a 2-day history of irritability, poor oral intake, and intermittent crying with her legs drawn up. She has had two episodes of loose stool and a low-grade fever. Her parents initially attributed the symptoms to gastroenteritis. She has no prior abdominal surgery. On examination she is distressed with handling and localises pain to the right lower quadrant when the examiner gently presses on the abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 155, RR 28, Temp 38.3 C, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Rigid abdomen with guarding in the right iliac fossa and suprapubic region. Decreased bowel sounds. No palpable mass. Rovsing sign positive.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 15.6), CRP 85 mg/L. Urinalysis: trace leucocytes, no nitrites.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral rehydration and observation for viral gastroenteritis
Abdominal X-ray to assess for obstruction or faecolith
Ultrasound abdomen and urgent paediatric surgical review
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast for diagnosis
IV antibiotics alone with plan for interval appendicectomy

stem: A 22-month-old girl presents with a 3-week history of progressive unsteadiness when walking and involuntary jerking movements of her limbs. Her parents describe chaotic eye movements that have worsened over the past week. She has become increasingly irritable and her sleep is disturbed. Prior to this she was developing normally. There is no history of recent infection or travel.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120, RR 24, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable child. Chaotic multidirectional conjugate saccadic eye movements (opsoclonus). Myoclonic jerks of the trunk and limbs. Truncal ataxia - unable to sit unsupported. Palpable firm non-tender 3 cm mass in the left flank. No hepatomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: FBC and UEC normal. LDH 320 U/L (mildly elevated).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation to identify the underlying cause?

options.text: Urine catecholamines and abdominal ultrasound
MRI brain and lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
EEG with prolonged monitoring for epileptic activity
CT chest and abdomen with IV contrast and biopsy
Anti-neuronal antibody panel and serum ferritin

subtopic_detail: Acute osteomyelitis - IV to oral switch criteria
stem: A 7-year-old boy was admitted 5 days ago with acute haematogenous osteomyelitis of the left distal tibia, confirmed on MRI. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. He has been receiving IV flucloxacillin since admission. His pain has improved significantly and he is now mobilising with crutches. He is tolerating oral fluids and food well.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, Temp 36.8 C (afebrile for 48 hours)
data_table.Investigations: Day 1: CRP 145 mg/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L. Day 5 (today): CRP 32 mg/L (trending down), WCC 10.4 x10^9/L. Blood cultures day 3: no growth (repeat).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in antibiotic management?

options.text: Continue IV flucloxacillin for a total of 14 days
Continue IV flucloxacillin until CRP normalises completely
Switch to oral cefalexin with CRP monitoring as outpatient
Switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 3 weeks total
Insert a PICC line for outpatient parenteral therapy

stem: A 5-year-old girl falls from monkey bars onto an outstretched hand. She presents with a swollen, painful left elbow held in flexion. On assessment she cannot make an 'OK' sign with her left hand - she is unable to flex the interphalangeal joint of her thumb or the distal interphalangeal joint of her index finger. She has intact radial and ulnar nerve function. Her radial pulse is palpable and capillary refill is 2 seconds in all fingers.

data_table.Examination: Marked swelling of the left elbow with ecchymosis anteriorly. Passive extension limited by pain. Unable to flex IPJ of thumb or DIPJ of index finger (anterior interosseous nerve). Intact thumb and finger extension, intact finger abduction and adduction. Radial pulse present, warm hand.
data_table.Investigations: X-ray left elbow: Gartland type III extension-type supracondylar fracture with posterior displacement of the distal fragment. Anterior humeral line does not intersect the capitellum.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this fracture?

options.text: Above-elbow backslab and orthopaedic review in 24 hours
Closed reduction and percutaneous K-wire fixation urgently
Collar and cuff sling with urgent nerve conduction studies
Fasciotomy of the forearm for suspected compartment syndrome
Urgent closed reduction with K-wires and AIN reassessment

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizures - metabolic workup and pyridoxine trial
stem: A 3-day-old term neonate develops recurrent multifocal clonic seizures that are refractory to two loading doses of phenobarbital. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, delivery was normal, and Apgar scores were 9 at 1 minute and 9 at 5 minutes. There were no risk factors for sepsis. The baby was well for the first 48 hours before seizures began.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 145, RR 42, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: BSL 3.8 mmol/L. Corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L. Magnesium 0.85 mmol/L. Sodium 139 mmol/L. FBC: WCC 12.4 x10^9/L, platelets 280 x10^9/L. Blood culture: pending. LP: clear CSF, WCC 2, protein 0.8 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L. Ammonia 45 micromol/L (normal). Cranial ultrasound: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empiric IV aciclovir for possible neonatal HSV encephalitis
IV pyridoxine trial with concurrent EEG monitoring
Third loading dose of phenobarbital to maximum level
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging sequences
Midazolam infusion for refractory status epilepticus

subtopic_detail: TTN versus RDS discrimination in late preterm
stem: A male infant is born at 35+2 weeks gestation by elective caesarean section for breech presentation. No antenatal corticosteroids were administered. Within 30 minutes of birth he develops grunting, nasal flaring, and subcostal recession. He is placed on CPAP at 7 cmH2O with FiO2 0.35.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, RR 72, SpO2 91% on room air (pre-CPAP), 96% on CPAP 7/0.35, Temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession. Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles. No focal wheeze.
data_table.Investigations: CXR at 2 hours: diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacification with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Blood gas (capillary): pH 7.28, pCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, BE -4, lactate 2.1 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency
Transient tachypnoea of the newborn from delayed clearance
Congenital pneumonia from ascending infection at birth
Meconium aspiration syndrome following in utero passage
Pneumothorax from barotrauma during initial resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent cyanotic heart disease - PGE1 initiation
stem: A 6-hour-old term neonate born in a rural hospital develops progressive cyanosis. The infant was well at birth with normal Apgar scores. Oxygen saturations were noted to be 72% on the routine newborn screen at 4 hours of age and have not improved with high-flow oxygen via nasal prongs. The infant is feeding poorly but is not in respiratory distress.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 155, RR 44, SpO2 72% right hand, 70% right foot on 2 L/min O2, Temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis. No respiratory distress. No murmur audible. Femoral pulses palpable. Liver not enlarged. Active and alert.
data_table.Investigations: Hyperoxia test: SpO2 74% and PaO2 35 mmHg after 10 minutes on 100% oxygen via headbox.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubation with mechanical ventilation at high FiO2
Urgent echocardiography before commencing any treatment
IV fluid bolus and broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis
IV prostaglandin E1 infusion and transfer to cardiac centre
Inhaled nitric oxide for persistent pulmonary hypertension

subtopic_detail: Protracted bacterial bronchitis - diagnosis and management
stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a persistent wet productive cough for 6 weeks. There is no wheeze, no night-time cough, and no exercise limitation. He has no personal or family history of atopy or asthma. He is thriving and has had no weight loss. He attends daycare and has had frequent upper respiratory infections this winter but this cough has persisted beyond his last URTI. A trial of salbutamol inhaler made no difference.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100, RR 22, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing child. No clubbing. Chest: transmitted upper airway sounds. No focal crackles or wheeze. No chest wall deformity.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: clear lung fields, no focal consolidation or lymphadenopathy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroid trial for 8 weeks for possible asthma
Sweat chloride test to exclude cystic fibrosis
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days with reassessment
CT chest and referral to paediatric respiratory physician
Reassurance and observation as this is likely post-viral cough

stem: A 14-month-old girl has had two febrile urinary tract infections in 6 months, both caused by Escherichia coli. After her second episode, a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) is performed and shows bilateral vesicoureteral reflux - grade II on the right and grade IV on the left with moderate left ureteric dilatation and blunting of the left renal calyces. A DMSA scan shows a 15% differential function defect in the left kidney with cortical scarring at the upper pole.

data_table.Investigations: MCUG: right VUR grade II, left VUR grade IV. DMSA scan: left kidney 35% differential function (normal > 45%), upper pole cortical scar. Right kidney 65% differential function, normal uptake.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Observation with prompt treatment of future symptomatic UTIs
High-dose intermittent antibiotic therapy for acute episodes only
Bilateral ureteric reimplantation surgery within 4 weeks
Endoscopic subureteric injection of bulking agent bilaterally
Continuous low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis with regular follow-up

stem: A 3-year-old girl is diagnosed with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis affecting her right knee and left ankle. She is ANA-positive at a titre of 1:640. She has no eye complaints, no redness of the eyes, and no photophobia. Her parents ask whether any additional screening is required.

data_table.Examination: Right knee: mild effusion, limited extension by 10 degrees. Left ankle: mild swelling, full range of motion. No enthesitis. No psoriatic rash. Eyes: no conjunctival injection on external examination.
data_table.Investigations: ANA positive 1:640. RF negative. HLA-B27 negative. ESR 28 mm/hr, CRP 12 mg/L.

lead_in: What is the most important additional screening for this child?

options.text: Slit-lamp ophthalmology review every 3 months for uveitis
Annual cardiac echocardiography for valvular involvement
Six-monthly renal function and urinalysis for nephritis
Baseline and 6-monthly DEXA scan for osteoporosis screening
Six-monthly liver function tests for methotrexate toxicity

stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with a 6-week history of a scaly erythematous rash on his scalp that has not responded to antifungal treatment. His parents also report increased thirst and frequent wet nappies over the past 3 weeks. On examination there is a palpable firm non-tender swelling over the right parietal bone. He has mild hepatomegaly and a seborrhoea-like rash involving the scalp, postauricular area, and groin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120, Temp 37.0 C, weight 12 kg (25th centile)
data_table.Examination: Scaly erythematous plaques on scalp, behind ears, and in inguinal folds. Firm 2 cm non-tender swelling right parietal region. Liver palpable 3 cm below costal margin. Spleen not palpable.
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 98 g/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L, platelets 145 x10^9/L. Urine specific gravity 1.002 (dilute). Serum sodium 147 mmol/L. Skull X-ray: well-defined lytic lesion right parietal bone with no sclerotic margin.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Skin scraping for fungal microscopy and culture
Biopsy of the skull lesion with CD1a immunohistochemistry
Whole-body MRI for metastatic neuroblastoma staging
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for leukaemia
Water deprivation test to confirm diabetes insipidus

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis - renal monitoring and biopsy threshold
stem: A 6-year-old boy was diagnosed with IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) 3 weeks ago with a typical purpuric rash over the lower limbs and buttocks, arthralgia, and colicky abdominal pain. His acute symptoms have resolved with supportive care. At routine follow-up today, his urine dipstick shows 2+ protein and 2+ blood. His blood pressure is 108/72 mmHg (above the 95th centile for age and height).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 90, BP 108/72 mmHg (>95th centile), Temp 36.6 C
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: protein 2+, blood 2+, no casts on microscopy. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (uPCR): 120 mg/mmol (normal < 20 mg/mmol). Serum creatinine 48 micromol/L (normal for age). Serum albumin 30 g/L (mildly low). Complement C3 and C4: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassurance and repeat urinalysis in 4 weeks as routine
Oral prednisolone and ACE inhibitor with nephrology review
Immunoglobulin A level and ANCA panel for reclassification
Renal biopsy and paediatric nephrology referral
IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy for 3 days

subtopic_detail: Acute pancreatitis in child - initial management
stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with acute onset epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, and anorexia for 12 hours. She has no prior abdominal complaints. She takes sodium valproate for epilepsy. On examination she lies still and resists any movement. Her abdomen is tender in the epigastrium with guarding but no rebound.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 24, Temp 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding. No distension. Bowel sounds reduced. No jaundice.
data_table.Investigations: Serum lipase 1450 U/L (normal < 60 U/L). Serum amylase 680 U/L (normal < 100 U/L). ALT 45 U/L. Bilirubin 15 micromol/L. Calcium 2.20 mmol/L. Triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L. Abdominal ultrasound: diffusely swollen pancreas with peripancreatic fluid. No gallstones. Common bile duct not dilated.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Urgent ERCP for suspected common bile duct obstruction
Commence total parenteral nutrition with bowel rest
Prophylactic IV antibiotics with imipenem for prevention
IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and early enteral feeding
Immediate surgical necrosectomy for pancreatic necrosis

subtopic_detail: OSA in child - adenotonsillectomy referral criteria
stem: A 5-year-old boy is referred by his GP for assessment of snoring. His parents report loud habitual snoring every night for the past 12 months, witnessed apnoeic pauses, restless sleep, and mouth breathing. He has daytime behavioural difficulties including inattention at school. His BMI is at the 75th centile. He has grade 3+ tonsillar hypertrophy bilaterally and chronic mouth breathing with adenoid facies.

data_table.Examination: Grade 3+ tonsillar hypertrophy bilaterally (tonsils meeting in the midline). High arched palate. Mouth breathing at rest. No pectus excavatum. BMI 75th centile.
data_table.Investigations: Overnight polysomnography: obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index (oAHI) 12 events/hour (normal < 1), SpO2 nadir 84%, peak end-tidal CO2 55 mmHg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intranasal mometasone spray for 12 weeks with review
CPAP therapy titration and long-term home CPAP use
Weight management program and repeat polysomnography in 1 year
Mandibular advancement device fitted by dental specialist
Referral for adenotonsillectomy with post-operative monitoring

stem: A 6-week-old infant presents with inspiratory stridor that has been present since 2 weeks of age. The stridor is worse during feeding and when the infant is supine. It improves when the infant is prone or calm. She is exclusively breastfed and feeding well, gaining weight along the 50th centile. There is no history of intubation or respiratory distress at birth.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 38, SpO2 98% on room air, Temp 36.8 C, weight 4.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest, worsening with agitation and feeding. No biphasic stridor. No subcostal recession at rest. No cyanosis. Good air entry bilaterally.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Flexible nasendoscopy in the outpatient ENT clinic
Lateral neck X-ray to assess the subglottic airway
CT neck with contrast for structural airway assessment
Microlaryngoscopy and bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
Barium swallow to assess for vascular ring compression

stem: A 10-year-old boy is referred by his GP for weight management. His BMI is 28.5 kg/m2, placing him above the 99th centile for age. He has acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck and axillae. His mother has type 2 diabetes. He has no symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea and is normotensive. He is Tanner stage 2 for pubic hair.

data_table.Vital signs: Height 143 cm (75th centile), weight 58.3 kg (>99th centile), BMI 28.5 kg/m2 (>99th centile), BP 112/68 mmHg (normal)
data_table.Examination: Acanthosis nigricans posterior neck and axillae bilaterally. Abdominal obesity. No striae. Normal external genitalia. Tanner stage 2.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial metabolic screening for this child?

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test and serum insulin level
Fasting lipids, glucose, HbA1c, and liver function tests
Thyroid function tests and early morning cortisol only
Leptin level and genetic testing for monogenic obesity
Overnight polysomnography and echocardiography screening

stem: A term neonate is born to a mother who was found to have reactive syphilis serology (RPR titre 1:64, TPPA positive) at 32 weeks gestation. She received a single dose of benzathine penicillin at 33 weeks but no further treatment or follow-up serology. The neonate appears well at birth but the paediatric team is called to assess for possible congenital syphilis.

data_table.Examination: Well-appearing term neonate. No rash. No hepatosplenomegaly. No rhinitis. Fontanelles soft and flat.
data_table.Investigations: Neonatal serology: RPR titre 1:32. FBC: Hb 165 g/L, WCC 14 x10^9/L, platelets 180 x10^9/L. LFTs: ALT 28 U/L, ALP 180 U/L (normal neonatal). Long bone X-rays: no periostitis or metaphyseal changes.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this neonate?

options.text: Observation only as maternal treatment was adequate
Repeat neonatal serology in 3 months for titre comparison
IV benzylpenicillin for 10 days with follow-up serology
Single dose IM benzathine penicillin to the neonate
Lumbar puncture only and treat based on CSF findings

subtopic_detail: Congenital long QT syndrome - neonatal management
stem: A 5-day-old term neonate is found to have a heart rate of 45 bpm during routine monitoring in the postnatal ward. An ECG shows 2:1 atrioventricular block with a ventricular rate of 48 bpm. The atrial rate is 96 bpm. The QTc interval on the ECG is measured at 620 ms. There is no maternal history of anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies. The mother has no history of syncope or cardiac arrest. The neonate is haemodynamically stable with good perfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 48 bpm, BP 58/35 mmHg (normal for neonate), SpO2 96%, Temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Well-perfused. No murmur. Liver not enlarged. Feeding well.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: atrial rate 96 bpm, ventricular rate 48 bpm. 2:1 AV block. QTc 620 ms (Bazett formula). Alternating T-wave morphology (T-wave alternans). Echocardiogram: structurally normal heart. Maternal anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies: negative.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Autoimmune congenital heart block - isoprenaline infusion
Neonatal myocarditis - IV immunoglobulin and supportive care
Electrolyte disturbance - IV calcium and magnesium correction
Congenital long QT syndrome - IV magnesium and beta-blocker
Congenital complete heart block - urgent pacemaker insertion

subtopic_detail: Macrophage activation syndrome complicating systemic JIA
stem: An 8-year-old girl with known systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) presents with high spiking fevers to 41 C that have become persistent rather than quotidian over the past 3 days. She has developed progressive confusion, bruising, and abdominal distension. Her sJIA has been managed with anakinra but she recently had a dose reduction. Her parents describe a 'different kind of sick' compared with her usual flares.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150, BP 90/55 mmHg, RR 32, Temp 40.8 C, SpO2 95%
data_table.Examination: Confused, GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Jaundiced. Hepatosplenomegaly. Scattered petechiae and bruising. Lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 2.8 x10^9/L (was 22 x10^9/L last week), Hb 88 g/L, platelets 45 x10^9/L. Ferritin 28,500 microg/L (was 800 microg/L last week). LDH 2,450 U/L. Triglycerides 5.8 mmol/L. Fibrinogen 0.9 g/L (low). AST 380 U/L, ALT 290 U/L. D-dimer 8.5 mg/L. ESR 8 mm/hr (paradoxically low).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase anakinra dose with addition of IV immunoglobulin
Empiric IV antibiotics and blood cultures for presumed sepsis
IV methylprednisolone pulse and ciclosporin with ICU admission
Fresh frozen plasma and platelet transfusion with observation
Etoposide-based chemotherapy per HLH-2004 protocol

stem: A 14-month-old boy presents with a 3-month history of developmental regression. He had been walking with support but has lost this skill and now has truncal hypotonia and can no longer sit unsupported. His parents describe episodic vomiting and lethargy, often during minor illnesses. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Family history reveals a maternal uncle who died at age 3 from an undiagnosed neurological condition.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Truncal hypotonia with appendicular spasticity. Nystagmus. Absent deep tendon reflexes. Intermittent dystonic posturing of the upper limbs. Growth parameters: weight 9.2 kg (10th centile, was 25th), length 75 cm (25th centile).
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 5.8 mmol/L (elevated). Pyruvate 0.08 mmol/L. Lactate-to-pyruvate ratio 72 (elevated, normal < 20). Plasma alanine elevated. CSF lactate 4.2 mmol/L (elevated, normal < 2.0 mmol/L). Urine organic acids: elevated lactate and Krebs cycle intermediates.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Whole exome sequencing including mitochondrial DNA analysis
Muscle biopsy with respiratory chain enzyme analysis
Skin fibroblast culture for respiratory chain enzyme assay
Electroencephalogram with prolonged monitoring for epilepsy
MRI brain with spectroscopy for characteristic lesion pattern

subtopic_detail: Inborn errors of metabolism - neonatal presentation
stem: A 5-day-old term neonate born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery is brought to the emergency department with poor feeding, vomiting, and progressive lethargy over the past 24 hours. The parents are first cousins. The newborn screening results are not yet available. The neonate is hypotonic with a weak cry. There is no rash, fontanelle is flat, and there are no dysmorphic features.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 55, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 36.4, Weight 3.2 kg
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.18, pCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3 10 mmol/L, lactate 5.2 mmol/L, anion gap 24 mmol/L; BSL 3.8 mmol/L; ammonia 680 micromol/L (ref <50); FBC: WCC 11.2, Hb 165 g/L, platelets 220; CRP <1 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Cease enteral feeds and commence IV 10% dextrose infusion
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg as a slow bolus
Start IV ceftriaxone and obtain blood cultures urgently
Arrange urgent haemodialysis for ammonia clearance
Commence oral sodium benzoate as an ammonia scavenger

stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after an 8-minute episode of left-sided rhythmic jerking associated with a fever of 39.2 degrees Celsius. The seizure was terminated with buccal midazolam by paramedics. She has been previously well with no developmental concerns and immunisations are up to date. On arrival she is drowsy but rousable to voice. The fontanelle is flat and soft. There is no neck stiffness, rash, or focal neurological deficit on examination. Tympanic membranes are dull bilaterally.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 155, RR 32, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 38.8 (post-midazolam)
data_table.Investigations: BSL 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with written febrile seizure safety advice
Perform a lumbar puncture once the child is more alert
Commence IV levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis now
Arrange an urgent CT brain before any further workup
Request an EEG within the next 24 hours for assessment

stem: An 8-year-old girl is referred to the paediatric outpatient clinic by her teacher, who reports multiple daily episodes of staring blankly for 5 to 10 seconds, during which she does not respond. The episodes have been occurring for three months and are increasing in frequency. Her mother reports occasional eyelid fluttering during the episodes. She is otherwise developmentally normal and has no history of tonic-clonic seizures. There is no significant medical or family history. An EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no dysmorphic features, growth on 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antiepileptic drug?

options.text: Carbamazepine 5 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
Sodium valproate 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
Ethosuximide 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally
Lamotrigine 0.5 mg/kg/day with slow titration upwards
Levetiracetam 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses orally

stem: A 6-year-old boy with known systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis on methotrexate and prednisolone presents with three days of worsening fever to 40 degrees Celsius, increasing lethargy, and a new petechial rash. His JIA had been in remission for 6 months. On arrival she is afebrile and her left hip examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165, BP 85/50 mmHg, RR 34, SpO2 95% RA, Temp 40.1
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 92 g/L, WCC 2.1 x10^9/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L; ESR 8 mm/hr (previously 65); CRP 180 mg/L; ferritin 18,400 microg/L; fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (ref 2.0-4.0); triglycerides 4.8 mmol/L; ALT 285 U/L; AST 420 U/L; LDH 1,850 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Increase the methotrexate dose to achieve disease control
Commence IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin for presumed sepsis
Commence urgent plasmapheresis for cytokine clearance
Administer high-dose IV etoposide as per HLH protocol
Commence IV methylprednisolone pulse therapy 30 mg/kg/day

stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department by his father who reports the baby 'rolled off the couch' approximately two hours ago. The infant is irritable and holds his right arm still. There are no bruises visible. Examination reveals swelling and tenderness of the right mid-humerus. X-ray shows a spiral fracture of the right humeral shaft. The father appears anxious and provides inconsistent accounts of the mechanism when asked again by the nurse.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, RR 38, SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.9
data_table.Investigations: X-ray right humerus: spiral mid-shaft fracture with no periosteal reaction; no other injuries visible on this film

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Make a mandatory notification to child protection services
Apply a splint and arrange orthopaedic follow-up this week
Request a skeletal survey before considering notification
Obtain coagulation studies and calcium to exclude pathology
Admit for observation and request social work consultation

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 24-hour history of refusal to bear weight on his left leg. He had an upper respiratory tract infection five days ago that has resolved. He is febrile at 38.9 degrees Celsius. Examination shows the left hip held in flexion and external rotation with marked pain on attempted internal rotation. He screams when the hip is passively moved. He is able to bear weight briefly on the right leg only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 28, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 38.9, Weight 15 kg
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, neutrophils 12.4; CRP 78 mg/L; ESR 42 mm/hr; hip ultrasound: moderate left hip joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe oral ibuprofen and reassess in 24 to 48 hours
Perform urgent ultrasound-guided hip joint aspiration
Commence IV flucloxacillin empirically without aspiration
Arrange MRI of the left hip to clarify the diagnosis first
Obtain a plain X-ray of the left hip and pelvis urgently

stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 3-week history of worsening left knee pain. He has a BMI of 32 kg/m2. He walks with an antalgic gait favouring the left side. On examination, the left knee has a full range of movement without effusion. When the left hip is flexed, it obligately externally rotates. Internal rotation of the left hip is limited to 10 degrees and reproduces his knee pain. The right hip examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 110/68 mmHg, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Left knee: no swelling, no tenderness, full ROM; Left hip: obligate external rotation on flexion, internal rotation 10 degrees (right 40 degrees), pain with log roll

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: X-ray of the left knee in two views as the pain localises there
Bilateral hip X-ray including anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral
MRI of the left hip to assess for avascular necrosis early
Ultrasound of the left hip to evaluate for a joint effusion
Blood tests including FBC, CRP, and ESR to exclude infection

stem: A 13-year-old girl with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 presents to the emergency department unable to weight-bear on her right leg after tripping on a step one hour ago. She reports two weeks of intermittent right groin aching prior to the fall. On examination, the right leg lies shortened and externally rotated. Any attempt to internally rotate or flex the hip causes severe pain. She is afebrile and her left hip examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105, BP 108/66 mmHg, Temp 36.6, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: AP pelvis X-ray: widened right proximal femoral physis with posterior displacement of the right femoral epiphysis; left hip normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Allow protected weight-bearing and arrange outpatient review
Commence traction and arrange semi-urgent orthopaedic review
Arrange urgent closed reduction under general anaesthesia today
Keep non-weight-bearing and arrange urgent in-situ screw fixation
Request MRI to assess femoral head vascularity before surgery

stem: An 11-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes at home. He has had gastroenteritis with vomiting and reduced oral intake for 36 hours. He was born at term with no neonatal complications. His newborn screening was reportedly normal. He has had two previous hospital presentations with hypoglycaemia during intercurrent illness at ages 4 and 8 months, both attributed to 'fasting intolerance' and managed with IV dextrose. On arrival he is drowsy and postictal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 40, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 37.2, Weight 9.5 kg
data_table.Investigations: BSL 1.2 mmol/L; VBG: pH 7.28, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L; urinary ketones: trace; FBC and UEC normal; LFTs: ALT 95 U/L, AST 110 U/L

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood triggered by fasting
Congenital hyperinsulinism with recurrent fasting episodes
Growth hormone deficiency causing recurrent hypoglycaemia
Adrenal insufficiency with cortisol deficiency during stress
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD)

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of widespread petechiae and bruising on her limbs and trunk. She had a viral upper respiratory tract infection two weeks ago that has fully resolved. She is well-appearing, afebrile, and active. There is no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. She has no bleeding from mucosal surfaces.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100, BP 95/60 mmHg, Temp 36.8, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 125 g/L, WCC 7.2 x10^9/L (normal differential), platelets 8 x10^9/L; blood film: reduced platelets, no blasts, normal red cell morphology; coagulation studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observation with activity restriction and close follow-up
Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for five to seven days
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as a single dose
Transfuse one unit of pooled platelets to reduce bleeding risk
Perform a bone marrow aspirate to exclude acute leukaemia

stem: A 9-month-old boy presents with 6 days of fever up to 39.5 degrees Celsius that has not responded to paracetamol or ibuprofen. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips, and irritability. He does not have a rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, or limb changes. All cultures and viral studies are negative. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165, RR 36, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 39.3
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, Hb 98 g/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L; CRP 125 mg/L; ESR 72 mm/hr; ALT 65 U/L; albumin 26 g/L; urinalysis: WCC 15/hpf, no growth on culture; blood cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care and reassess in 24 to 48 hours
Commence high-dose aspirin and arrange outpatient echocardiography
Request urgent echocardiography and administer IVIG 2 g/kg
Start empiric IV antibiotics for possible occult bacterial focus
Obtain a CT angiogram of the coronary arteries for assessment

stem:
A 16-day-old male infant born at term is brought to the emergency department with poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy over the past 3 days. The parents report increasing drowsiness and two episodes of dusky spells. The newborn screening result collected on day 3 has not yet been returned. On examination, the infant is dehydrated with mottled skin, delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds, and appears shocked.

The external genitalia appear normal male with bilaterally descended testes. There is hyperpigmentation of the scrotum and nipples noted by the parents as present from birth.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 185, RR 60, SpO2 92% RA, Temp 36.2, Weight 3.0 kg (birth weight 3.4 kg)
data_table.Investigations: BSL 1.8 mmol/L; VBG: pH 7.22, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 12 mmol/L, K+ 7.8 mmol/L, Na+ 118 mmol/L; FBC: Hb 180 g/L, WCC 14.2, platelets 310

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia with salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Late-onset neonatal sepsis with secondary adrenal suppression
Pyloric stenosis with secondary dehydration and electrolyte loss
Congenital renal tubular acidosis with potassium retention
Congenital heart disease with cardiogenic shock and end-organ failure

stem: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents who are concerned about episodic inconsolable crying and pallor. The episodes last 2 to 3 minutes and occur every 15 to 20 minutes. Between episodes the infant appears lethargic but is not distressed. He had a viral gastroenteritis one week ago that resolved. He has had one loose stool with a red-tinged mucoid appearance. On examination the abdomen is soft between episodes but the infant draws up his knees and screams during an observed episode.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150, RR 34, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 37.0
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft between episodes, no distension, no palpable mass, red-tinged mucoid stool on nappy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain abdominal X-ray in supine and erect views urgently
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast for detailed assessment
Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for a target or doughnut sign
Proceed directly to therapeutic air enema without prior imaging
Obtain stool cultures and viral PCR to identify the causative agent

stem: A 10-year-old boy with no prior medical history presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and 4 kg weight loss. He is now vomiting and has Kussmaul breathing. He is alert and oriented. His weight is 32 kg. He has been given a 10 mL/kg 0.9% NaCl bolus for mild dehydration. His blood glucose is 28 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 32 (deep), SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.9, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.12, pCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3 8 mmol/L, K+ 5.2 mmol/L; BSL 28 mmol/L; ketones (blood) 5.8 mmol/L; Na+ 131 mmol/L (corrected Na+ 137); UEC: creatinine 65 micromol/L

lead_in: After the initial bolus, what is the most appropriate fluid and insulin strategy?

options.text: 0.9% NaCl at 5 mL/kg/hr with insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr started after 1 hour of fluids
0.9% NaCl at maintenance plus 5% deficit over 48 hours, insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hr after 1 hour
0.9% NaCl at maintenance plus 5% deficit over 48 hours, insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr after 1 hour
0.45% NaCl at maintenance rate with insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr started immediately after bolus
0.9% NaCl at maintenance plus 7% deficit over 24 hours, insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hr after 1 hour

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a 5-day history of bloody diarrhoea followed by 2 days of decreasing urine output and pallor. She attended a petting zoo one week before symptom onset. On examination she is pale with periorbital oedema. She has not received any antibiotics during this illness. Stool culture has returned positive for Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli O157:H7.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, BP 108/72 mmHg (above 95th centile), RR 28, Temp 37.1
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 72 g/L, WCC 14.8 x10^9/L, platelets 38 x10^9/L; blood film: schistocytes present, helmet cells; UEC: creatinine 280 micromol/L (baseline ~30), urea 22 mmol/L, K+ 5.9 mmol/L, Na+ 132 mmol/L; LDH 2,400 U/L; haptoglobin <0.1 g/L; reticulocyte count elevated

lead_in: Which of the following interventions should be specifically avoided?

options.text: Platelet transfusion to correct the severe thrombocytopenia
Packed red cell transfusion to maintain haemoglobin above 70 g/L
IV fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid for rehydration
Antibiotic therapy targeting the Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
Renal replacement therapy if oliguria persists or K+ rises

stem: A 5-week-old first-born male infant presents with a 10-day history of progressively forceful, non-bilious vomiting that now occurs after every feed. His mother describes the vomit as projectile. He is hungry immediately after vomiting. He has lost 200 g from his 2-week weight check. On examination he is mildly dehydrated with a sunken fontanelle. A firm olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant during a test feed. Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis with a pyloric muscle thickness of 5 mm and channel length of 18 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, RR 42, SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.8, Weight 3.6 kg
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.52, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 38 mmol/L, K+ 2.8 mmol/L, Na+ 133 mmol/L, Cl- 82 mmol/L (ref 98-106)

lead_in: What must be corrected before surgical intervention?

options.text: The metabolic acidosis, to reduce anaesthetic cardiac risk
The thrombocytopenia, to reduce the risk of surgical bleeding
The hypernatraemia, to prevent intraoperative seizures
The hypoglycaemia, to provide adequate energy for healing
The hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with IV fluids

subtopic_detail: Acute cerebellar ataxia vs posterior fossa tumour
stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of progressive unsteadiness and frequent falls. He had chickenpox (varicella) 10 days ago that has resolved. His parents report he was walking normally before this. On examination he has truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, and bilateral dysmetria. His speech is normal and there is no nystagmus. He is afebrile, alert, and interactive. There is no papilloedema on fundoscopy. He has no headache or vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99% RA, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, bilateral dysmetria on finger-nose, no nystagmus, no papilloedema, no cranial nerve deficit, normal tone and power in all limbs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose acute cerebellar ataxia and discharge with GP follow-up
Commence IV aciclovir for possible varicella cerebellitis urgently
Administer IV dexamethasone for presumed cerebellar inflammation
Arrange MRI brain to exclude a posterior fossa mass lesion
Perform lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis or encephalitis

stem: A 7-week-old former 38-week infant presents to a metropolitan paediatric emergency department in winter with 4 days of coryza and 24 hours of worsening work of breathing. He has been refusing feeds for 8 hours and has had 3 short apnoeas witnessed in triage. He is on standard nasal-prong oxygen at 1 L/min. RSV PCR is positive. He has had no fever above 38.0 degrees C and chest X-ray shows hyperinflation without focal consolidation. The treating registrar has commenced him on 2 L/kg/min heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula with FiO2 0.4 thirty minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 78, SpO2 89% on HFNC FiO2 0.4, temperature 37.6 degrees C, CRT 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession, head bobbing, fine crackles bilaterally, mottled peripheries
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.24, pCO2 64 mmHg, HCO3 26, lactate 2.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue current HFNC settings and reassess in 30 minutes
Trial nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with reassessment at 15 minutes
Order an urgent CT chest and consult paediatric infectious diseases
Administer IV salbutamol 5 mcg/kg over 10 minutes and reassess
Escalate to non-invasive ventilation with PEEP 6 cmH2O and contact PICU

subtopic_detail: Hypokalaemia during continuous salbutamol in acute asthma
stem: A 7-year-old girl with acute severe asthma has had one hour of continuous nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and oral prednisolone. Her work of breathing is improving. She is tremulous.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 164, RR 32, SpO2 95 percent on 4 L/min oxygen
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.34, pCO2 36 mmHg, lactate 4.1 mmol/L, potassium 2.7 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add potassium to the intravenous fluid and continue salbutamol
Stop the salbutamol and give intravenous magnesium sulfate instead
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and repeat the venous gas
Halve the salbutamol dose and start an insulin dextrose infusion
Withhold further treatment and repeat the venous gas in four hours

stem: A 22-month-old boy presents to a regional emergency department at 0200 with 6 hours of barking cough, stridor at rest and increased work of breathing. You diagnose moderate to severe croup and give 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone and a single 5 mL nebulised 1:1000 adrenaline dose. Forty-five minutes later he is markedly improved with no stridor at rest, normal effort, and is settled in his mother's arms. The drive to home is 35 minutes and the family is reliable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No stridor at rest, occasional barky cough, normal work of breathing, alert
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home immediately with safety-netting advice and GP review
Observe for a further 3 hours after the nebulised adrenaline before discharge
Admit to the short-stay unit for overnight observation regardless of progress
Repeat nebulised adrenaline and observe for 30 minutes before discharge
Administer a second oral dexamethasone dose 0.6 mg/kg and discharge

stem: A 13-month-old girl presents to a metropolitan ED with 3 days of fever to 39.2 degrees C, cough and tachypnoea. She is fully immunised including 13-valent pneumococcal vaccine and is otherwise well. Vital signs are stable, she has mild hypoxia, and the chest X-ray shows right-sided lobar consolidation. She tolerates oral intake. Mother asks whether she should be on hospital antibiotics or take something home. The closest hospital pharmacy is open. The referring GP queried whether macrolide cover is needed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, RR 48, SpO2 93% room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, focal crackles right base, no wheeze, alert and feeding
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe consolidation, no effusion. CRP 88 mg/L. Nasopharyngeal viral PCR pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days as a macrolide-first strategy
Oral amoxicillin + clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days
Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days, review in 48 hours
IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours admitted for 48 hours then oral
Oral cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days as broader cover

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease: incomplete criteria + IVIG timing
stem:
A 14-month-old previously well boy of Korean background is brought in on day 6 of fever above 39 degrees C. The fever has not responded to paracetamol. On examination he has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue, and an ill-defined truncal rash. He has only one cervical lymph node measuring 1.2 cm and no extremity changes. His hands and feet look normal.

Mother has Googled and asks if this could be Kawasaki disease. The locum registrar argues he does not meet 4 of 5 classic criteria, so cannot have Kawasaki disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, RR 30, SpO2 99%, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, ill-defined truncal rash, one 1.2 cm cervical node, hands and feet unremarkable, irritable
data_table.Investigations: CRP 95 mg/L, ESR 62 mm/hr, WCC 17.4 x10^9/L (neutrophil predominant), platelets 580 x10^9/L, ALT 52 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urine WCC 35 x10^6/L sterile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents, treat as viral illness, review in 48 hours
Arrange echocardiography and give IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus aspirin
Take blood cultures and start empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily
Give a single IV methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg as first-line therapy
Wait until day 10 of fever and re-evaluate the criteria before treating

stem: A 14-month-old boy has just completed a 7-day course of cefalexin for his first culture-confirmed febrile urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli sensitive to amoxicillin and cefalexin. He defervesced within 48 hours of antibiotics. Antenatal scans were normal. He is now well, growing along the 50th centile, voiding normally and feeding well. Mother asks about follow-up imaging because his older brother had a renal scan.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 28, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, abdomen soft and non-tender, no flank tenderness, external genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture pre-treatment: E. coli, sensitive to amoxicillin and cefalexin. Post-treatment urine culture not done.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up imaging plan?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks; escalate only if abnormal
Micturating cystourethrogram now and DMSA scan at 6 months
DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to assess for renal scarring
Daily trimethoprim prophylaxis with no further imaging arranged
No additional imaging is required; counsel parents on prompt presentation for any future fever and arrange GP follow-up

stem: A 4-year-old girl is admitted with viral gastroenteritis and has been on 0.45 percent saline plus 5 percent dextrose maintenance for the past 18 hours. On the morning ward round she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that does not stop after 90 seconds. She has had 4 episodes of vomiting overnight. Her admission sodium was 137 mmol/L. The bedside finger-prick glucose is 5.2 mmol/L. IV access is patent. She weighs 16 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 36, SpO2 95% on 4 L/min Hudson mask, temperature 36.9 degrees C, BP 92/56
data_table.Examination: Ongoing tonic-clonic seizure, pupils 3 mm equal, no focal features, mottled extremities
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.32, Na 122 mmol/L, K 3.8, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, lactate 2.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 20 minutes
IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg and switch maintenance to 0.9% saline
IV 3% sodium chloride 3 mL/kg bolus over 10 minutes
IV mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 20 minutes for cerebral oedema
IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg load and continue current maintenance fluid

stem: A 7-month-old girl is brought to a tertiary emergency department after a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes that occurred 90 minutes ago at home during a febrile illness. She is fully immunised including pneumococcal and Hib vaccines. She is currently alert and feeding. Her admission temperature is 39.0 degrees C. There is no rash, neck stiffness or bulging fontanelle. She has not been on antibiotics. The intern proposes a lumbar puncture; the registrar disagrees.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 39.0 degrees C, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Alert, feeding, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no neck stiffness, no rash, no focal neurology, no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L, urine dipstick pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture immediately before further treatment is started
Observe for 4 hours and perform LP if signs of meningitis emerge
Start empirical IV ceftriaxone and discharge after 1 hour
Arrange urgent CT head to exclude raised intracranial pressure
Discharge home with safety-net advice and antipyretic plan immediately

stem: A 4-year-old boy with a known structural focal epilepsy is brought to a metropolitan ED in a generalised convulsive seizure that has lasted 12 minutes. He received 0.5 mg/kg buccal midazolam from his mother at home 9 minutes ago and a further 0.15 mg/kg IV midazolam 5 minutes ago without effect. He weighs 16 kg. IV access is patent. He is hypoxic on facemask oxygen. There is no history of cardiac disease or pre-existing QT prolongation. The team are preparing the next IV agent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 28 irregular, SpO2 91% on 8 L/min facemask, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Ongoing tonic-clonic activity, eyes deviated right, no focal lateralisation, pupils 4 mm equal sluggish
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L, ABG drawn

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next agent?

options.text: IV levetiracetam 40 mg/kg infusion over 5 minutes
IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading dose over 20 minutes
Repeat IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg as a third dose
IV thiopentone 4 mg/kg with rapid sequence intubation
IV sodium valproate 40 mg/kg over 5 minutes

stem:
A breastfed term male newborn (40 weeks, birthweight 3.4 kg) is reviewed at 60 hours of life on the postnatal ward. He has visible jaundice to the upper chest. Antenatal blood group was O Rhesus positive; baby's group has not been checked. There is no family history of haemolytic disease. He is feeding 3 hourly and has had 4 wet nappies in the past 24 hours.

Total serum bilirubin (TSB) returns at 312 micromol/L. The local phototherapy threshold chart shows the 60-hour line for a low-risk term infant at 320 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice to upper chest, alert, good tone, suck strong, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: TSB 312 micromol/L (conjugated 8 micromol/L), Hb 178 g/L, blood group not yet determined, DAT pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence phototherapy immediately and recheck TSB in 6 hours
Discharge home with community midwife review in 48 hours
Arrange immediate exchange transfusion in the next 12 hours
Switch from breast milk to formula and recheck TSB in 24 hours
Recheck TSB in 6 to 12 hours and reassess against threshold

stem: A 3-year-old boy weighing 16 kg is brought to a metropolitan ED 4 hours after his mother saw him chewing ferrous sulfate 325 mg tablets from her bedside table. She estimates he ate between 10 and 15 tablets. He has vomited twice and had 1 episode of bloody diarrhoea. A 4-hour serum iron level returns at 92 micromol/L. Anion gap is 22. The poisons information centre has been notified. IV access is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 32, BP 84/52, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C, CRT 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Pale, peripheries cool, lethargic but rousable, abdomen tender, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Serum iron 92 micromol/L at 4 hours, VBG pH 7.27 lactate 5.4 mmol/L, anion gap 22, glucose 4.8 mmol/L, abdominal X-ray: scattered radio-opaque tablets in stomach

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV desferrioxamine 15 mg/kg/hour titrated for 24 hours
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally and observe for 24 hours
Gastric lavage and oral N-acetylcysteine for 21 hours
Whole-bowel irrigation only and recheck iron at 8 hours
IV sodium bicarbonate infusion to correct acidaemia

stem:
A 5-year-old boy weighing 20 kg presents to a regional ED 35 minutes after eating cashew nuts at a birthday party. He developed urticaria, lip swelling and wheeze within minutes. He received IM adrenaline 0.15 mg from a school EpiPen Junior 15 minutes ago. On arrival you give a second IM adrenaline 0.3 mg into the lateral thigh, supine positioning, oxygen, and IV fluid 20 mL/kg.

He now has resolved wheeze, no stridor, and normal effort. His parents are asking when they can go home; the trip is 90 minutes by car.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 102/64, RR 26, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Residual mild lip swelling, no wheeze, no stridor, no rash now, alert and engaging
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated acutely

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition plan?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days and discharge
Discharge home now with a new EpiPen prescription and GP follow-up
Admit overnight for 24-hour observation regardless of clinical course
Administer IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and discharge in 1 hour
Observe in monitored bed for at least 4 hours from second adrenaline dose

subtopic_detail: Otitis media: antibiotic threshold in Aboriginal child
stem: A 2-year-old Aboriginal boy living in a remote Northern Territory community is brought to the community clinic with 36 hours of fever, ear pulling, and irritability. He has had two previous episodes of acute otitis media this year. Both tympanic membranes are red and bulging, and the left is now perforated with mucopurulent discharge. He is otherwise well-perfused. His weight is 12 kg. The community-controlled health organisation has telephone access to a remote paediatrician.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral red bulging TMs, left perforation with discharge, no mastoid tenderness, no neck stiffness, mild rhinorrhoea
data_table.Investigations: Tympanocentesis swab obtained from discharging ear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Watchful waiting with paracetamol; review at 48 hours
Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days, then review
Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops alone for the perforated ear
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days
Single IM ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg with no oral follow-on course

stem:
A 12-year-old boy with a BMI on the 97th centile is brought to a metropolitan ED with 6 weeks of intermittent left thigh and knee pain, worse in the past 4 days. He has not had a fever. He can weight-bear with a limp. On examination he holds the left leg in external rotation; passive internal rotation of the left hip is restricted.

Plain radiographs (AP and frog-leg lateral) of both hips show widening of the left physis and a Klein line that does not intersect the femoral head epiphysis. He has no headaches and his blood pressure is normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 86, BP 124/78, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Externally rotated left lower limb, restricted internal rotation, no warmth or erythema, no effusion clinically, intact distal neurovascular status
data_table.Investigations: AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis - widened left physis with Klein line not intersecting epiphysis, no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with crutches and orthopaedic clinic review in 2 weeks
Admit, strict non-weight-bearing, urgent orthopaedic surgery review
MRI hip electively to characterise the slip before referral
Trial of weight-bearing rest, analgesia and review in 1 week
Aspirate the hip joint to exclude underlying septic arthritis

stem: A 5-year-old previously well boy is brought to a metropolitan ED with 36 hours of right hip pain and refusal to weight-bear. He had a viral URTI 1 week ago that has now resolved. His mother gave him paracetamol overnight; the fever has reduced. On examination he holds the hip in mild flexion and external rotation, and resists log-roll. The orthopaedic registrar asks for blood tests before any imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 24, SpO2 99%, temperature 38.4 degrees C now (was 38.8 overnight)
data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed and externally rotated, log-roll painful, no overlying erythema, no other joints involved
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.5 x10^9/L, CRP 38 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/hr

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with NSAIDs and orthopaedic review at 48 hours
Start empirical IV flucloxacillin and discharge in 24 hours
Hip ultrasound and urgent orthopaedic review for joint aspiration
MRI pelvis as the first imaging investigation undertaken
Reassure as transient synovitis and arrange home physiotherapy

stem: A 5-week-old male first-born infant is admitted with 10 days of progressive non-bilious vomiting after feeds. He weighs 3.8 kg (birthweight 3.5 kg). His mother reports a palpable 'olive' was felt during the abdominal examination. Ultrasound confirms pyloric channel length 18 mm and muscle thickness 5 mm. The paediatric surgical registrar plans pyloromyotomy. The anaesthetic team has asked you to optimise him pre-operatively. He has had no urine output in the past 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, BP 78/48
data_table.Examination: Mildly sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, CRT 3 sec, abdomen soft, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 mmol/L, K 2.8, Cl 88, HCO3 36, urea 9.4, creatinine 42, glucose 4.8, VBG pH 7.52 pCO2 50

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to pyloromyotomy within the next two hours
IV 0.9% saline bolus then K-containing maintenance; surgery once Cl above 100
IV Hartmann's solution at maintenance with theatre scheduled in 12 hours
Acetazolamide 5 mg/kg to pharmacologically correct the metabolic alkalosis
Nasogastric thickened feeding with review at 48 hours and home discharge

stem: A 10-month-old boy presents to a tertiary paediatric ED with 14 hours of intermittent inconsolable crying, drawing his legs up, and 2 episodes of redcurrant jelly stool. He is currently well-perfused, has had 4 wet nappies overnight, but is pale and drawn. Abdominal examination shows a tender right upper quadrant sausage-shaped mass; the right iliac fossa feels empty. Ultrasound shows a target sign at the hepatic flexure with no free fluid and no signs of perforation. He has not had a fever or vomiting. Surgical and radiology teams are available on-site.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 32, BP 92/58, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, CRT 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: RUQ sausage-shaped mass, no peritonism, no bruises, no abdominal distension, alert when not in pain
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, lactate 1.2 mmol/L, abdominal US: target sign at hepatic flexure, no free fluid, no perforation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Conservative management with NG decompression and IV fluids only
Laparotomy and manual reduction without attempted air enema
Barium enema reduction without surgical team on standby
Air enema reduction under fluoroscopy with surgical standby
CT abdomen with IV contrast to confirm before any intervention

stem:
A 5-month-old boy is brought to a metropolitan ED by his mother with 12 hours of irritability and one episode of vomiting. There is no history of trauma. On examination he has a posterior left torus skull fracture identified on CT brain after the registrar noticed a small bruise on the scalp. He has a healing right tibial fracture identified incidentally.

His parents have provided inconsistent accounts of how the bruise occurred. He is otherwise well-perfused and feeding. There are no overlying skin marks suggestive of birthmarks, and Mongolian spots are absent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 32, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8 degrees C, alert
data_table.Examination: Healing right tibial fracture identified incidentally, small left scalp bruise, posterior left skull fracture on CT, no retinal haemorrhages yet examined
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coagulation normal, CT brain: torus skull fracture, no intracranial bleed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home with paediatric outpatient follow-up in 1 week
Order coagulation studies only and re-review in 24 hours
Discuss with the family alone before notifying child protection
Admit, notify child protection, skeletal survey and ophthalmology
Refer to outpatient social work without admission or notification

stem: A 9-year-old boy with congenital chronic kidney disease (eGFR 28) presents to a metropolitan ED with weakness and palpitations. His ECG shows peaked T waves and widening QRS at 130 ms with no P waves visible. His last potassium 3 weeks ago was 5.4 mmol/L. He weighs 28 kg and is on captopril and a low-potassium diet. Mother reports he ate a banana and orange juice for breakfast. IV access is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92 (irregular), RR 22, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Reduced peripheral tone, alert, no focal neurology, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urgent VBG K 8.2 mmol/L, Na 134, ionised calcium 1.10, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, lactate 1.4, ECG: peaked T waves, QRS 130 ms, no P waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first intervention?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg without IV intervention
IV insulin 0.1 unit/kg with 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose over 30 minutes
IV calcium gluconate 10% 0.5 mL/kg over 5 minutes
IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg as the first intervention
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) 1 g/kg orally

stem: A 4-year-old previously well boy presents with 3 weeks of pallor, intermittent fever, bony aches in the lower limbs at night, and easy bruising. His mother noted petechiae on his shins this morning. He has been refusing to walk for the past 2 days. On examination he has cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and scattered bruises. He has no rash on his face. He is otherwise stable. His FBC and metabolic panel return abnormal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 26, BP 102/64, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy 1 to 2 cm, hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin, splenomegaly 6 cm, scattered bruises on shins, petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Hb 64 g/L, WCC 42 x10^9/L (blasts on film), platelets 12 x10^9/L, urate 0.62 mmol/L, K 5.6, phosphate 2.4, calcium 1.95, LDH 1850 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day immediately in the ED
Transfuse platelets to above 100 then discharge for outpatient haematology
Transfer to a paediatric oncology unit with IV fluids and allopurinol
Bone marrow aspirate in ED by the on-call medical registrar
Arrange CT chest and abdomen, broad-spectrum antibiotics, 24 hour review

stem: A 3-week-old infant is brought to a metropolitan ED with 5 days of progressive coughing paroxysms ending in apnoea and cyanosis, followed by a high-pitched inspiratory whoop. Her older sister (4 years) had a prolonged cough for 3 weeks but has not been tested. The mother had pertussis vaccine 4 years ago but was not boosted in this pregnancy. Pernasal pertussis PCR is positive. There is a 7-week-old cousin in the same household. The infant is admitted to the high-dependency unit on continuous monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 between paroxysms, RR 60 with paroxysms, SpO2 92% off oxygen, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coughing paroxysms with cyanosis, post-tussive vomiting, otherwise alert
data_table.Investigations: Pertussis PCR positive, FBC: lymphocytosis 18 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial plan?

options.text: Supportive care only; pertussis self-limits and antibiotics do not alter course
Amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for the infant, no contact treatment
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the infant, no contact prophylaxis given
Azithromycin for the infant plus prophylaxis to all household contacts under 6 months
Erythromycin 40 mg/kg/day for the infant in the first month of life

subtopic_detail: Late preterm sepsis vs HSV: empirical cover
stem: A 9-day-old late-preterm female infant (born at 35 weeks, now home with mother) presents to a metropolitan ED with 12 hours of poor feeding, increased sleeping, temperature 38.1 degrees C and a single brief generalised seizure witnessed in the waiting room. Mother had genital ulcers diagnosed at 36 weeks as first-episode genital herpes; no antiviral suppression was given. There is no other relevant maternal history. Capillary glucose is 3.6 mmol/L. The neonatal team has been called. IV access is patent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 64, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C, BP 64/36 (low for age)
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, anterior fontanelle flat, mottled extremities, post-ictal but rousable, no rash currently visible
data_table.Investigations: FBC, blood culture, CSF, urine sent. Capillary glucose 3.6 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial cover?

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin only
IV cefotaxime plus amphotericin B only
IV flucloxacillin plus gentamicin only
IV vancomycin plus cefotaxime only
IV ampicillin plus cefotaxime plus aciclovir

stem:
A 4-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of progressively worsening shortness of breath and a tight, non-productive cough. He has a known history of atopy, including eczema and a peanut allergy, and has had two previous hospital admissions for viral-induced wheeze. His parents report he had a coryzal illness starting three days ago. He received six puffs of salbutamol via a spacer every three hours at home with minimal effect.

On examination, he is alert but agitated, sitting forward and speaking in single words. He has a prominent tracheal tug, severe intercostal recessions, and widespread biphasic wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally. He is immediately commenced on high-flow oxygen, continuous nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium bromide, and intravenous hydrocortisone. One hour later, he remains severely distressed with poor air entry.

data_table.Vital signs: Initial: HR 165 bpm, RR 48/min, SpO2 90% (room air). Current (1hr): HR 175 bpm, RR 45/min, SpO2 92% (8 L/min O2 mask)
data_table.Examination: Agitated, single words, severe work of breathing, poor air entry.
data_table.Medications: Continuous nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone given in ED.

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Administer a stat dose of intramuscular adrenaline.
Commence an intravenous continuous aminophylline infusion.
Intubate and commence mechanical ventilation immediately.
Administer a single bolus of intravenous magnesium sulfate.
Administer a fluid bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride.

stem:
A 4-week-old male infant is brought to the clinic by his mother, who is concerned about his persistent yellowish skin discolouration. He was born at 39 weeks gestation. The infant is exclusively breastfed, feeding every 3 hours, and producing 6 - 8 wet nappies per day. His stools have become noticeably pale and chalky over the past week, and his urine leaves a dark yellow stain on the nappy.

On examination, the infant is alert and vigorous, with a weight of 4.2 kg (birth weight 3.4 kg). He has frank scleral icterus and widespread cutaneous jaundice extending to the umbilicus. Abdominal examination reveals a smooth, firm liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, RR 35/min, Temp 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: Total Bilirubin 210 micromol/L, Conjugated Bilirubin 145 micromol/L, ALT 85 U/L, AST 90 U/L, GGT 410 U/L, ALP 550 U/L, Hb 145 g/L, DAT negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the mother and continue exclusive breastfeeding.
Commence intensive blue-light phototherapy immediately.
Prescribe a trial of oral ursodeoxycholic acid.
Arrange an outpatient hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan.
Admit for an urgent fasting abdominal ultrasound.

stem:
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by ambulance at 22:00 after texting her friend that she 'took a whole packet of pills'. Her mother found empty blister packs of paracetamol (500 mg tablets, 24 pack) and ibuprofen (200 mg tablets, 24 pack) on her bed. The patient is tearful and refuses to confirm exactly when she took the tablets, but her mother states she was last seen well at 15:00 when she returned from school.

She has a history of major depressive disorder and is prescribed fluoxetine 20 mg daily, which she takes intermittently. On examination, she is alert and orientated. She complains of mild nausea and generalised abdominal pain, but abdominal examination is soft and non-tender. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with a QTc of 410 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 bpm, BP 115/70 mmHg, RR 16/min, Temp 36.8 C, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Alert. Mild nausea. Abdomen soft, non-tender.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: Normal sinus rhythm, QTc 410 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence an intravenous acetylcysteine infusion immediately.
Administer 50g of activated charcoal orally or via nasogastric tube.
Measure serum paracetamol level and plot on the nomogram.
Observe closely and check liver function tests in 12 hours.
Commence an intravenous infusion of sodium bicarbonate.

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother, who states he rolled off a 50 cm high bed onto a carpeted floor two hours ago. He is previously healthy and meeting appropriate developmental milestones, though he is not yet walking.
