Since the fall, he has been extremely irritable, refusing to bear weight, and crying whenever his right leg is moved during nappy changes.

On examination, his right thigh is swollen and exquisitely tender to palpation. A secondary survey reveals multiple small bruises in varying stages of healing over his central back and abdomen. A plain radiograph of the right lower limb is obtained, revealing a classic bucket-handle (metaphyseal corner) fracture of the distal femur. No other acute injuries are identified on initial assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 145 bpm, RR 30/min, Temp 37.0 C, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Right thigh swollen and tender. Bruising (various ages) on torso.
data_table.Investigations: XR Right Leg: Metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal femur.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Apply a hip spica cast and arrange outpatient orthopaedic follow-up.
Perform a bone mineral density scan to rule out osteogenesis.
Admit for a skeletal survey and notify child protection services.
Reassure the mother as this is consistent with the reported fall.
Obtain an urgent CT head to rule out abusive head trauma.

stem:
A 3-year-old girl is rushed to the emergency department by ambulance. Her parents report a 12-hour history of high fever, extreme lethargy and vomiting. On arrival she is poorly responsive, groaning to pain. She is notably pale with mottled skin and a non-blanching purpuric rash spreading rapidly across her lower limbs and abdomen. Her extremities are cold to the touch with a capillary refill time of 5 seconds.

Two wide-bore intravenous cannulae are immediately secured and a point-of-care lactate returns 5.0 mmol/L. No antibiotics, fluids or vasoactive agents have yet been given. The senior registrar is selecting the single best next intervention.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170 bpm, BP 70/40 mmHg, RR 40/min, Temp 39.5 deg C, SpO2 92% on room air.
data_table.Examination: Obtunded (GCS 9). Cold peripheries, mottled. Spreading purpuric rash.
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas: pH 7.20, pCO2 35 mmHg, lactate 5.0 mmol/L, BSL 4.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention in this first hour?

options.text: Take blood cultures, give IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg and 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus now and reassess perfusion within minutes
Perform immediate rapid sequence endotracheal intubation in the resuscitation cubicle before starting any antibiotic or fluid therapy
Commence a peripheral intravenous adrenaline infusion as the single first intervention before antibiotics or any fluid bolus
Administer a 10 mL/kg bolus of 4% human albumin solution as the initial fluid choice for resuscitation in this child
Administer a stat dose of intravenous hydrocortisone sodium succinate as the single initial intervention now to address possible adrenal insufficiency

stem: A 10-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 18 months ago is brought to the emergency department after 24 hours of vomiting and lethargy. His insulin pump tubing disconnected overnight and he has had progressive abdominal pain and thirst since morning. He received a correction bolus by pen 2 hours ago. On arrival he is drowsy but obeys commands. During initial treatment with isotonic fluids and intravenous insulin, he becomes increasingly irritable and complains of severe headache. His mother reports he is now asking repetitive questions. Capillary glucose has fallen from 28.6 mmol/L to 18.2 mmol/L over 90 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 30/min deep respirations, Temp 37.1 C, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Dry mucosa, delayed capillary refill 3 seconds, new confusion and reduced orientation
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.08, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.9 mmol/L, Na 131 mmol/L, K 4.7 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Continuous insulin infusion commenced, isotonic fluids running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Reduce insulin infusion rate and repeat venous blood gas in 30 minutes before further action
Administer hyperosmolar therapy and urgently escalate for presumed cerebral oedema
Increase isotonic fluid replacement because persistent dehydration is the likely explanation
Arrange urgent CT brain before initiating further treatment to confirm diagnosis
Cease insulin and commence dextrose-containing fluids as the glucose is falling rapidly

stem:
A 10-month-old boy presents to ED with 8 hours of intermittent screaming episodes, drawing up of the legs and repeated non-bilious vomiting. Between episodes he is pale and settles briefly but has become increasingly lethargic. His mother reports a mild viral illness last week. He was born at term, has had no previous surgery and is fully immunised. He is afebrile, mildly dehydrated, with a soft but mildly distended abdomen.

A small amount of red mucus is seen in the nappy after a pain episode. There is no bilious vomiting and no peritonism. HR 156, RR 30, BP 86/54, SpO2 99 percent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.2 deg C, HR 156 bpm, RR 30/min, BP 86/54 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Intermittent colicky pain, mild abdominal distension, no guarding, no palpable hernia
data_table.Investigations: Nil yet
data_table.Medications: No regular medicines; no known drug allergies

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step and how should management proceed if the imaging is positive?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound now; if a target sign with doughnut or pseudokidney appearance is seen and no peritonitis or perforation, proceed to air-contrast enema reduction after surgical consult
Plain abdominal x-ray and treat empirically as gastroenteritis with oral rehydration and antiemetics in the short-stay observation ward area
Urgent upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation with volvulus, without prior ultrasound
CT abdomen with IV contrast as the initial imaging modality
Stool PCR for infectious gastroenteritis and observe in short stay, without abdominal imaging

stem:
A 7-year-old girl receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents with fever and malaise. She had her last vincristine and dexamethasone cycle 6 days ago and now has worsening tiredness, reduced oral intake, and mild abdominal discomfort. Her central venous line is clean at the skin but has not been accessed in 2 days. She takes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis and ondansetron as needed.

Her parents report no cough, sore throat, or urinary symptoms, but she had one episode of loose stool this morning. On examination she looks unwell but is not in respiratory distress. She is pale, has cool peripheries, and appears tachycardic.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.1 deg C, HR 148 bpm, RR 26/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Tired, pale, cool peripheries, central line site clean, abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 0.7 x10^9/L, neutrophils 0.1 x10^9/L, platelets 62 x10^9/L, Hb 88 g/L; CRP 96 mg/L; lactate 2.7 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, ondansetron PRN, chemotherapy 6 days ago

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately
Observe for 4 hours and repeat FBC before treating
Start oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and discharge if stable
Remove the central venous line before cultures are taken
Give granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and await marrow recovery

stem: A 13-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes is brought in with 18 hours of abdominal pain, vomiting, and increasing lethargy after a viral illness. She has missed two doses of insulin because she was not eating well and thought it would be safer to stop it. Her mother says she has been drinking large volumes of water and passing urine frequently for 2 days. She is drowsy but rousable, has deep breathing, and smells strongly of ketones.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.4 deg C, HR 132 bpm, RR 30/min with Kussmaul pattern, BP 94/60 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucous membranes, tachypnoea, fruity breath, capillary refill 3 s, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: BGL 31.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.14, HCO3 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, Na 130 mmol/L, K 5.5 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Start insulin infusion immediately without fluids
Give a normal saline bolus and begin the paediatric ketoacidosis protocol
Administer subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin and discharge if ketones fall
Give sodium bicarbonate because the pH is below 7.20
Treat hyperkalaemia with calcium gluconate before any fluids

stem:
An 8-month-old ex-35-week infant is brought to the emergency department in winter with 4 days of cough, coryza, and poor feeding. He was reviewed by a GP yesterday and diagnosed with bronchiolitis. Overnight he took less than half his usual feeds and had two episodes of post-tussive vomiting. His mother reports increasing work of breathing and fewer wet nappies today.

He has no history of congenital heart disease but required CPAP briefly after birth. In the emergency department he is started on low-flow oxygen via nasal prongs with transient improvement in saturations. Thirty minutes later he remains tachypnoeic with persistent subcostal and intercostal recession. Capillary blood gas shows mild hypercapnia without acidosis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 62/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, Temp 37.8 C, SpO2 89% room air improving to 93% on 2 L/min oxygen
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, diffuse crackles with scattered wheeze, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: CBG pH 7.34, pCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: No regular medications, immunisations up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence high-flow nasal prong therapy and continue supportive management with nasogastric hydration
Trial inhaled salbutamol and reassess respiratory rate before considering respiratory support escalation
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone because the hypercapnia suggests developing bacterial pneumonia
Arrange urgent intubation because preterm birth increases risk of sudden respiratory decompensation
Discharge home with frequent oral fluids because oxygen saturations improved on nasal prongs

stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department with fever, vomiting, and progressive lethargy over 12 hours. His parents report he complained of leg pain earlier today and became difficult to wake after an afternoon nap. On arrival he is confused and intermittently agitated. A blanching maculopapular rash on his trunk has evolved over the past hour into scattered non-blanching purpuric lesions over the lower limbs. Peripheral IV access is difficult and blood cultures have not yet been obtained. During assessment he develops cool peripheries and prolonged capillary refill.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.7 C, HR 168 bpm, RR 36/min, BP 76/42 mmHg, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Confused, mottled skin, purpuric rash over legs, neck stiffness difficult to assess, capillary refill 5 seconds
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.24, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 4.9 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: No regular medications, no known drug allergies

lead_in: What is the single best next step in management?

options.text: Perform urgent lumbar puncture before antibiotics because CSF confirmation will guide therapy duration
Administer empiric intravenous ceftriaxone immediately while initiating aggressive septic shock resuscitation
Obtain blood cultures and CT brain before antimicrobial therapy because altered consciousness raises concern for raised ICP
Commence aciclovir and transfer for MRI because a viral CNS cause is more likely here
Administer intramuscular benzylpenicillin and observe response before escalating to intravenous therapy

stem:
A 13-year-old boy with moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency department with worsening shortness of breath over 8 hours after developing rhinorrhoea and cough 2 days earlier. He used salbutamol every 2 hours overnight with progressively shorter relief. On arrival he can speak only in short phrases and prefers to sit upright. He receives inhaled salbutamol and ipratropium with oral dexamethasone.

Ninety minutes later he remains tachypnoeic with increasing fatigue. Air entry is now reduced bilaterally and wheeze is quieter than at presentation. A venous blood gas is repeated because nursing staff are concerned he appears more drowsy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 bpm, RR 38/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 91% on room air improving to 94% with oxygen
data_table.Examination: Marked accessory muscle use, reduced bilateral air entry, quieter wheeze, intermittent drowsiness
data_table.Investigations: Initial VBG pH 7.37 pCO2 39 mmHg, repeat VBG pH 7.29 pCO2 56 mmHg
data_table.Medications: Repeated inhaled salbutamol and ipratropium, oral dexamethasone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue intermittent salbutamol only because the oxygen saturation has improved with supplemental oxygen
Arrange discharge with prednisolone because reduced wheeze indicates treatment response
Escalate to intensive care review for intravenous therapy and possible respiratory support
Administer intravenous antibiotics because viral-triggered bacterial pneumonia is now most likely
Cease bronchodilators and commence non-invasive ventilation on the ward because tachycardia suggests toxicity

stem: A 7-week-old previously healthy girl presents with fever and reduced feeding for 10 hours. She was born at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery and required no neonatal admission. Her mother reports increased sleepiness and only two wet nappies since morning. There is no cough, rhinorrhoea, vomiting, or diarrhoea. On examination the infant briefly opens her eyes to stimulation but settles quickly back to sleep. Peripheral perfusion is mildly delayed. Urinalysis obtained by catheter specimen shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 C, HR 178 bpm, RR 44/min, BP 82/48 mmHg, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild lethargy, delayed capillary refill 3 seconds, soft fontanelle, no increased work of breathing
data_table.Investigations: WCC 17.8 x10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L, urinalysis positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with oral cefalexin because a urinary source is the likely cause of fever
Commence empiric intravenous antibiotics and admit for full septic evaluation and observation
Observe in the emergency department without antibiotics until blood culture results become available
Arrange renal ultrasound before treatment because structural urinary abnormalities are likely
Repeat observations after paracetamol because fever alone may explain the tachycardia and lethargy

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the ED with 14 hours of fever, headache, vomiting, and increasing irritability. His parents say he was well yesterday but became sleepy and complained of pain when the room was bright. On examination he is drowsy but rousable, with neck stiffness and photophobia. He has a blanching maculopapular viral exanthem over his trunk, but no purpuric rash.

His capillary refill is 3 seconds, and he is more tachycardic than expected. The registrar is considering lumbar puncture, but the child looks increasingly unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.6 deg C, HR 154 bpm, RR 28/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, neck stiffness, photophobia, no focal neurology, capillary refill 3 s
data_table.Investigations: Nil yet
data_table.Medications: No regular medicines; no known drug allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture immediately before any antibiotics
Take blood cultures and start empirical intravenous antibiotics
Observe for 2 hours and repeat neurological examination
Give oral ibuprofen and discharge with safety-netting
Arrange CT brain before deciding on antibiotics

stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to an after-hours clinic with refusal to use his right arm since being collected from childcare this afternoon. His mother says he was playing on a low couch when he started crying, but she did not witness any major fall. He has had one previous ED attendance for a bruised cheek, explained as a collision with a toy box.

He is otherwise well, with no fever or systemic symptoms. On examination he is holding the elbow slightly flexed and pronated, and he cries when the forearm is supinated. There is no obvious deformity, but there is a faint bruise on the upper arm. He is fully immunised and has no relevant past medical history. The clinician wonders whether this is a nursemaid's elbow or whether the bruising means something more concerning.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 deg C, HR 112 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Refuses to use arm, mild tenderness, faint upper arm bruise, no swelling, no deformity
data_table.Investigations: Nil yet
data_table.Medications: No regular medicines; no known drug allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attempt reduction of a pulled elbow
Order dedicated limb radiographs and document the bruising carefully
Discharge with reassurance because there is no deformity
Provide oral ibuprofen and review in the morning
Apply a sling and treat as a viral synovitis

stem:
A 14-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department with episodic distress and vomiting for 9 hours. His parents report sudden periods of screaming and drawing his knees to his chest lasting 1 to 2 minutes, followed by lethargy and apparent exhaustion. Earlier today he tolerated small sips of fluid but has since vomited twice, most recently with bilious content.

He had a mild viral upper respiratory illness 4 days ago. On arrival he appears pale and intermittently drowsy between episodes of pain. During examination he becomes irritable and inconsolable before settling again. Shortly afterwards the child passes a small stool mixed with blood and mucus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 bpm, RR 30/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, Temp 37.2 C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Intermittent abdominal guarding, mild abdominal distension, palpable sausage-shaped mass in right upper quadrant
data_table.Investigations: VBG lactate 2.8 mmol/L, glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral rehydration therapy and observe because viral gastroenteritis remains the most likely diagnosis
Arrange urgent air enema reduction after surgical consultation and initial stabilisation
Request urgent CT abdomen because the palpable abdominal mass suggests malignancy
Proceed directly to laparotomy because bilious vomiting confirms bowel perforation
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone because occult bacteraemia commonly presents with episodic abdominal pain

stem:
A 3-year-old boy presents with persistent fever for 6 days. He was initially diagnosed with viral infection by a local clinic after developing conjunctival injection and irritability. Over the following days he developed cracked lips, reduced oral intake, swelling of the hands and feet, and a polymorphous truncal rash. Yesterday he began refusing to walk because of discomfort in his feet.

In the emergency department he is miserable and difficult to console but alert. There is no cough or coryza. Cervical lymphadenopathy is present on the left side.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.4 C, HR 148 bpm, RR 26/min, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, oedematous hands and feet, diffuse rash
data_table.Investigations: CRP 132 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hr, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, platelets 390 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue supportive management because thrombocytosis has not yet developed and diagnosis remains uncertain
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin with echocardiography assessment
Isolate and commence vitamin A because incomplete measles vaccination makes measles the most likely diagnosis
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone because persistent fever with cervical lymphadenopathy suggests occult sepsis
Delay treatment until coronary artery abnormalities are confirmed on echocardiography

stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought in after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. He has had 4 days of cough, fever, and reduced appetite, and his parents have been encouraging large volumes of water because he 'did not want to drink milk'. He has been more sleepy since morning and vomited once before the seizure. On arrival he is postictal but arousable. He is not meningitic and has no focal neurology. His chest examination suggests a lower respiratory infection, but he has no wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.5 deg C, HR 124 bpm, RR 30/min, BP 98/62 mmHg, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Examination: Postictal, no focal deficit, no meningism, chest crackles at the right base
data_table.Investigations: Serum sodium 119 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: No regular medicines; no known drug allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Restrict fluids and repeat sodium in 6 hours
Give 3% hypertonic saline for symptomatic sodium derangement
Start oral sodium chloride and observe on the ward
Treat as febrile seizure and discharge once alert
Administer desmopressin to reduce urinary water loss

stem:
A 7-year-old boy presents with worsening abdominal pain and a rash over 4 days. One week earlier he had a mild upper respiratory illness that resolved spontaneously. His parents initially noticed small red-purple spots over his ankles and buttocks, followed by swelling around both knees. Today he developed intermittent crampy abdominal pain severe enough to wake him overnight and has vomited twice.

On examination he is uncomfortable but alert. The rash is palpable and non-blanching. His knees and ankles are mildly swollen but not erythematous. Urinalysis performed at triage demonstrates new microscopic haematuria and proteinuria.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.1 C, HR 118 bpm, BP 126/82 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over lower limbs and buttocks, mild periarticular swelling, diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis positive blood and protein, creatinine 74 micromol/L, platelets 338 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which finding most strongly indicates need for closer inpatient monitoring in this child?

options.text: Recent upper respiratory infection preceding the onset of rash and joint symptoms
Palpable purpura involving the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the lower limbs
Microscopic haematuria with elevated blood pressure despite preserved creatinine
Mild periarticular swelling affecting both knees and ankles without erythema
Intermittent crampy abdominal pain associated with two episodes of vomiting

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with sudden severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 5 hours ago. On arrival he walks hunched over and appears distressed. Examination shows a swollen tender left hemiscrotum with the testis lying slightly higher than the right. Cremasteric reflex is absent on the left. Urinalysis is negative for leukocytes and nitrites.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 C, HR 112 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 18/min
data_table.Examination: High-riding tender left testis, absent left cremasteric reflex, swollen hemiscrotum
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for infection markers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral antibiotics for epididymitis and arrange outpatient ultrasound review
Arrange urgent scrotal ultrasound before referral because imaging confirmation is required prior to surgery
Refer immediately for urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum
Attempt manual detorsion and discharge if the pain improves significantly afterwards
Observe with serial examinations because the absence of fever reduces the likelihood of surgical pathology

stem:
A 5-month-old boy presents during winter with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhoea, and poor feeding. Today his parents noticed increased work of breathing and reduced wet nappies. He was born at term with no neonatal complications. His older sibling recently had a viral upper respiratory illness. On arrival he is alert but feeding poorly and taking only half his usual volumes.

Examination reveals diffuse crackles and wheeze bilaterally with moderate subcostal recession. A medical student asks whether salbutamol nebulisers should be trialled because wheeze is prominent on auscultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.8 C, HR 154 bpm, RR 54/min, BP 88/50 mmHg, SpO2 90% room air
data_table.Examination: Moderate work of breathing, diffuse crackles and wheeze, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence supplemental oxygen and supportive care with feeding assessment
Administer repeated salbutamol nebulisers because wheeze indicates likely reactive airways disease
Commence oral prednisolone because moderate respiratory distress predicts steroid responsiveness
Arrange chest radiography because diffuse crackles suggest bacterial pneumonia requiring antibiotics
Discharge home after nasal suction because oxygen saturations commonly fluctuate during viral illnesses

stem:
A 7-year-old boy with known moderate persistent asthma presents to the emergency department with an acute exacerbation. He has had a coryzal illness for 3 days, and his asthma has been worsening despite increasing his fluticasone propionate preventer to 250 mcg BD and using salbutamol 6 puffs via MDI and spacer every 2-3 hours. On arrival, he is unable to complete sentences in one breath, speaking only 2-3 words at a time.

He is sitting upright with marked suprasternal and intercostal recession, and audible expiratory wheeze. His RR is 42, HR is 135 bpm, and SpO2 is 90% on room air. His PEFR is unmeasurable due to poor technique.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 42, HR 135 bpm, SpO2 90% RA, Temp 37.2°C, BP 105/65 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Unable to complete sentences (2-3 words), sitting upright, marked suprasternal and intercostal recession, audible expiratory wheeze, PEFR unmeasurable
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed at this stage
data_table.Medications: Fluticasone propionate 125 mcg BD (usual); Salbutamol 6 puffs via MDI + spacer given by mother prior to arrival

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management in the emergency department?

Hudson mask oxygen 8 L/min to SpO2 >94%, nebulised salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 250 mcg by O2-driven nebuliser, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg, repeat 20 min
High-flow nasal prong oxygen at 2 L/kg/min, IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg, urgent chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia before any bronchodilator therapy commences now
IV magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 min as first-line, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg, nasal prong O2 at 2 L/min to maintain SpO2 >92%
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg alone via O2-driven nebuliser, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg, observe one hour, then add ipratropium and consider IV therapy

A 9-month-old boy presents with a 12-hour history of episodic severe abdominal pain. His mother describes him drawing his knees up to his chest, screaming, and then becoming pale and lethargic for 10-15 minutes between episodes. He has vomited several times, initially milk and later bile-stained fluid. He passed a small amount of dark red stool mixed with mucus an hour ago.

On examination he appears pale and lethargic. His abdomen is distended with a vague sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are high-pitched. His heart rate is 160 bpm, temperature 37.5°C, and capillary refill time 3 seconds. He has not received rotavirus vaccine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160 bpm, Temp 37.5°C, RR 40, CRT 3 sec, BP 85/50 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Pale, lethargic, distended abdomen, sausage-shaped mass RUQ, high-pitched bowel sounds, currant jelly stool described

options.text: Abdominal X-ray (supine and erect)
Abdominal ultrasound
Contrast enema (barium or water-soluble)
CT abdomen with intravenous contrast
Diagnostic laparoscopy

stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the GP with a 1-week history of progressive periorbital swelling, most noticeable in the mornings. His mother has also noticed his clothes becoming tighter and his shoes not fitting. He has had a mild upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago. Urinalysis in the clinic shows 4+ protein and no blood. On examination he has periorbital oedema and pitting oedema of both legs to the knees.

His blood pressure is 95/55 mmHg (50th centile). His weight is 19 kg (previously 16 kg at his last well-child check 6 months ago). He has no rash, his abdomen is distended with a fluid thrill, and his testes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 95/55 mmHg (50th centile), HR 100 bpm, RR 24
data_table.Examination: Periorbital oedema, pitting oedema to knees, abdominal distension with fluid thrill, weight gain 3 kg, normal BP, no rash, normal testes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: 4+ protein, no blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology for renal biopsy to confirm the histological subtype before commencing any therapy
Oral prednisolone 60 mg/m2/day (about 40 mg daily) for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m2 alternate days for 4 weeks, with low-salt diet
Oral furosemide twice daily with strict 800 mL/day fluid restriction to manage the oedema, no corticosteroid therapy
IV 20% albumin over 4 hours followed by IV furosemide, then start oral prednisolone once oedema resolves
Oral enalapril daily to reduce proteinuria and observe for spontaneous resolution as likely post-infectious glomerulonephritis

stem:
An 8-year-old girl presents with 2 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss and 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and drowsiness. She is thin, dehydrated and responds only to pain (GCS 11, E2V3M6). She has Kussmaul breathing with RR 36, HR 140, BP 90/55, CRT 3 seconds and very dry mucous membranes. Weight 24 kg (estimated pre-illness 28 kg).

VBG: pH 7.05, pCO2 18, HCO3 5. Glucose 28 mmol/L. Ketones over 6 mmol/L. Na 130, K 5.2, urea 10.5, creatinine 90. There is no other significant history.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, BP 90/55 mmHg, RR 36 (Kussmaul), GCS 11, CRT 3 sec, Temp 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Thin, severe dehydration (~14% weight loss), drowsy, Kussmaul breathing, very dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.05, pCO₂ 18, HCO₃⁻ 5; Glucose 28 mmol/L; Ketones >6 mmol/L; Na⁺ 130, K⁺ 5.2, Urea 10.5, Cr 90

lead_in: Which initial intravenous fluid plan?

options.text: 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 15 minutes, repeat once if still in shock, then maintenance plus deficit replacement at 10 mL/kg/hour using 0.45% saline with potassium

10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 30 minutes, then calculate fluid deficit (about 7-10 percent of body weight cap) and replace half the deficit plus 24 hours of maintenance in the first 24 hours and the remainder over the next 24 hours, using 0.9% saline plus 40 mmol/L potassium once urine output is confirmed; start insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour at least 1 hour after fluids begin; monitor for cerebral oedema
Rapid 40 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline over 1 hour to restore circulating volume, then replace deficit over 24 hours
Commence IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately before any fluid bolus, with maintenance 0.9% saline and 5% dextrose
IV 0.9% saline at maintenance rate plus a 10 mL/kg bolus, with IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the acidosis

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of high fever, irritability, and vomiting. Her parents report she has been difficult to rouse for the past hour and has developed a new rash on her legs that does not fade when pressed with a glass. On examination she is drowsy, responding only to painful stimuli (GCS 9).

She is tachycardic at 170 bpm, hypotensive with BP 70/40 mmHg, capillary refill time 5 seconds, and peripheries are cold and mottled. There is a purpuric rash over her lower limbs and buttocks, with several lesions >2 mm. She has neck stiffness but no photophobia. Her temperature is 39.8°C.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.8°C, HR 170 bpm, BP 70/40 mmHg, RR 40, SpO₂ 94%, GCS 9, CRT 5 sec, cold mottled peripheries
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, purpuric rash lower limbs/buttocks (non-blanching, >2 mm), neck stiffness, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: None performed yet
data_table.Medications: Fully immunised including MenB and MenACWY

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture and blood cultures before antibiotics, then commence IV benzylpenicillin 4-hourly
Administer IV ceftriaxone immediately (max 2 g), take blood cultures, and commence IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus repeated as needed
Obtain an urgent CT brain to exclude cerebral oedema before lumbar puncture, then perform LP and start IV antibiotics
Administer IV dexamethasone 20 minutes before antibiotics, then give IV ceftriaxone and IV fluids, to reduce the risk of neurological sequelae
Notify the public health unit and await their advice before administering antibiotics, as this presentation is a notifiable condition requiring coordinated public health intervention

stem:
A 2-week-old male infant is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after his parents witnessed him stop breathing, become pale, and go limp while sleeping. The episode lasted approximately 20 seconds and resolved spontaneously when his mother picked him up and rubbed his back. He had been feeding well prior to the event and has not had any similar episodes.

He was born at 35+2 weeks gestation and spent 1 week in the special care nursery for feeding difficulties and mild respiratory distress, from which he recovered fully. He has been home for 1 week. On examination, he is alert, active, and feeding normally. His observations are: temperature 36.8°C, heart rate 140 bpm, respiratory rate 38, SpO₂ 98% on room air.

There are no dysmorphic features, and the neurological examination is normal. His weight is 2.6 kg (birth weight 2.5 kg). The infant is currently in the emergency department short stay unit and has been observed for 2 hours with no further events.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8°C, HR 140 bpm, RR 38, SpO₂ 98% RA, BP 70/40 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Alert, active, normal neurology, no dysmorphism, well hydrated, feeding normally
data_table.Investigations: None performed yet. Parents describe a 20-second apnoeic, pale, limp episode resolved spontaneously with tactile stimulation.

lead_in: According to Australian guidelines, what is the most appropriate disposition for this infant?

options.text: Discharge home with a home apnoea monitor, education on safe sleeping and CPR, and arrange a next-day follow-up with the GP and maternal child health nurse
Admit to hospital for cardiorespiratory monitoring for a minimum of 24 hours, with a 12-lead ECG, and consider pertussis PCR and other investigations only if clinically indicated
Perform a full septic workup including lumbar puncture, commence empiric IV antibiotics, and admit to the neonatal unit for a minimum 48 hours of observation
Arrange an urgent outpatient polysomnography (sleep study) and reflux study, and discharge home with strict return precautions and a nasal cannula oxygen setup
Refer to child protection services immediately as a BRUE in a preterm infant is highly suspicious for non-accidental injury, and admit for a skeletal survey and ophthalmology review

stem:
A 3-year-old boy with previous mild intermittent croup presents at 2200 with a barking cough and stridor at rest. He has moderate subcostal and suprasternal recessions. SpO2 93 percent on room air, HR 130, RR 32, T 37.4 deg C. The clinician calculates a Westley score of 4 (moderate). He is given oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000.

Within 30 minutes his stridor at rest resolves and he looks comfortable. He has been observed for 1 hour. The ED registrar is now considering disposition.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO₂ 93% initially, HR 130 bpm, RR 32
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest, moderate recessions, improved after adrenaline
data_table.Investigations: None

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate minimum observation period after the LAST adrenaline dose, and what condition supports safe discharge?

options.text: 1 hour after the LAST adrenaline dose, then discharge if stridor-free at rest with no recessions and normal work of breathing today
2 hours after the LAST adrenaline dose, then discharge if stridor-free at rest with no recessions and normal work of breathing today
Minimum 3 hours after the LAST adrenaline with the child stridor-free at rest, no recessions, comfortable on room air, tolerating fluids, with written safety-net advice
6 hours unconditionally after the LAST adrenaline dose, regardless of clinical status or work of breathing on examination today
No specific observation period required; discharge once stridor-free at rest regardless of time since the last adrenaline today

stem: A 6-year-old boy with known asthma presents with acute severe exacerbation. He has received 3 doses of nebulised salbutamol (5 mg) and ipratropium (250 mcg) over 1 hour, plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. His SpO₂ remains 89% on high-flow oxygen, he speaks in single words, and has severe recessions. Chest is tight, and air entry is reduced.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO₂ 89% on O₂ 15 L/min, HR 150 bpm, RR 40
data_table.Examination: Single words, severe recessions, reduced air entry bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: None
