options.text: Administer IV magnesium sulfate (max 2 g) over 20 minutes
Commence IV salbutamol infusion and transfer to ICU
Repeat the nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium every 20 minutes for another hour
Give an IV fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg and reassess
Obtain a chest X-ray to exclude pneumothorax

stem: A term infant is born at 39+2 weeks by vaginal delivery to a mother who had a temperature of 38.2°C during labour, with ruptured membranes for 20 hours. GBS screening at 36 weeks was negative. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (benzylpenicillin) was commenced only 2 hours before delivery. The infant appears well at birth, Apgars 9 and 9, and has remained asymptomatic for 6 hours in the postnatal ward.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, RR 45, Temp 36.9°C, SpO₂ 98%
data_table.Examination: Alert, normal tone, no respiratory distress, normal perfusion
data_table.Investigations: Maternal temp 38.2°C, ROM 20 hr, GBS negative, IAP given 2 hr before delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan for this infant?

options.text: Observe in hospital for 24-48 hours with regular clinical assessments; no antibiotics or bloods required
Perform a full septic workup including blood culture, FBE, CRP, and lumbar puncture, and commence IV antibiotics
Perform blood culture, FBE, and CRP at 6-12 hours of age; if CRP is normal and cultures negative at 48 hours, discontinue antibiotics if started, with close observation

Commence IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin empirically after taking blood culture and CRP, monitor clinically, and review at 36-48 hours; discontinue antibiotics if cultures negative, CRP normal, and infant remains well
Observe for 12 hours; if the infant remains well, discharge home at 24 hours with an early follow-up by the maternal child health nurse

stem:
A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of a palpable purpuric rash on his lower limbs and buttocks, diffuse colicky abdominal pain, and swelling of both knees and ankles. On examination, he is afebrile, HR 90 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg (90th centile for age). The rash is non-blanching and palpable. His abdomen is tender but soft. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and 2+ blood on dipstick.

A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) is 250 mg/mmol (normal <20). Serum creatinine is 45 µmol/L, and albumin is 32 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/70 (90th centile), HR 90, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpuric rash lower limbs/buttocks, swollen knees and ankles, tender abdomen, mild periorbital oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urine: 3+ protein, 2+ blood; UPCR 250 mg/mmol; serum Cr 45, albumin 32 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management of his renal involvement?

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology for consideration of renal biopsy and possible corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy, as he has nephrotic-range proteinuria
Commence oral prednisolone daily for 4 weeks to treat the nephritis and prevent long-term renal impairment
Discharge home with advice to monitor urine dipstick weekly for 6 weeks, as most cases of this nephritis resolve spontaneously without treatment
Start an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (enalapril) to reduce proteinuria and control blood pressure
Admit for intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy daily for 3 days, as severe nephritis in this setting requires immediate high-dose steroids

stem:
A 12-year-old girl with known cystic fibrosis (ΔF508 homozygous) presents with a 2-day history of crampy abdominal pain, distension, and bilious vomiting. She has not opened her bowels for 3 days, whereas normally she passes 2-3 loose stools daily despite pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (Creon 10,000 units/kg/day). She had an admission for distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS) 2 years ago, which resolved with conservative management.

On examination, she is afebrile, HR 100 bpm, BP 100/65 mmHg. The abdomen is distended, tympanic to percussion, and tender in the right lower quadrant with a palpable faecal mass. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Erect abdominal X-ray shows faecal loading in the distal ileum and caecum with no free air and no air-fluid levels. A Gastrografin enema performed in the emergency department shows a meconium-like material obstructing the distal ileum without complete obstruction.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100 bpm, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 22, Temp 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Distended, tender abdomen, palpable faecal mass RLQ, hyperactive bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: AXR: faecal loading distal ileum/caecum, no free air, no air-fluid levels; Gastrografin enema: impacted material in distal ileum without complete obstruction
data_table.Medications: Creon 10,000 U/kg/day, inhaled tobramycin, dornase alfa

lead_in: What is the most appropriate non-operative therapy for this episode of DIOS?

options.text: Oral polyethylene glycol 3350 (Movicol) sachets daily with increased fluids and continued pancreatic enzymes
Oral Gastrografin (diatrizoate meglumine) 50 mL diluted in 200 mL water, with IV fluids if vomiting persists
Nasogastric N-acetylcysteine 10 mL of 20% solution four times daily to break down the inspissated mucus plugs
Lactulose 10 mL three times daily plus a phosphate enema per rectum to stimulate colonic evacuation
Intravenous metoclopramide 8-hourly with continuous nasogastric suction, nil by mouth 48 hours

stem:
A 3-year-old Aboriginal girl presents with 24 hours of right ear pain, fever (38.4°C), and irritability. She attends daycare and has had three previous episodes of acute otitis media in the past 12 months, each treated with antibiotics. She is up to date with immunisations including the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. On otoscopy, the right tympanic membrane is bulging, erythematous, and has lost the normal light reflex.

The left tympanic membrane is normal. She has a runny nose and mild cough. She is otherwise well, taking oral fluids. Her mother is concerned about recurrent infections and requests antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4°C, HR 110 bpm, RR 26, SpO₂ 98%
data_table.Examination: Bulging, erythematous right TM, normal left TM, nasal discharge, no mastoid tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Not required
data_table.Medications: None currently; three prior AOM courses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?

options.text: No antibiotics; advise symptomatic management with paracetamol and review in 48 hours if not improved
Oral amoxicillin three times daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for 5 days
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for 7 days
Intramuscular ceftriaxone daily for 3 days

stem:
A 4-week-old male infant presents with a 10-day history of cough that began as mild coryza and has progressed to paroxysms of coughing followed by apnoeic pauses and post-tussive vomiting. The cough is non-productive, and he becomes cyanotic during the spells. On examination, the infant is alert but tachypnoeic with RR 50, SpO₂ 90% during a coughing paroxysm, HR 180 bpm.

Between paroxysms, SpO₂ is 97%. Chest auscultation reveals transmitted upper airway sounds but no crackles. There is no fever. A nasopharyngeal aspirate for Bordetella pertussis PCR is positive. Full blood count shows WCC 45 ×10⁹/L with lymphocyte predominance (70%), haemoglobin 140 g/L, platelets 480 ×10⁹/L.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 50, SpO₂ 90% during paroxysm, HR 180, Temp 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Paroxysmal cough with apnoea and cyanosis, post-tussive vomiting, transmitted upper airway sounds, no crackles
data_table.Investigations: NP aspirate: B. pertussis PCR positive; WCC 45, lymphocytes 70%, Hb 140, Plt 480

lead_in: What is the most important aspect of management?

options.text: Commence oral azithromycin daily for 5 days to reduce infectivity, and manage apnoeic episodes with careful monitoring in hospital
Initiate exchange transfusion or leukapheresis to reduce the white cell count, as extreme leukocytosis (>50 x10^9/L) is associated with fatal pulmonary hypertension
Commence IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg to neutralise pertussis toxin, as the toxin mediates the severe disease
Start oral prednisolone daily to reduce airway inflammation and prevent apnoeic spells
Provide continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) via nasal prongs to splint the airways and reduce apnoea frequency

stem:
A 22-month-old fully immunised boy is brought to his GP with 12 hours of fever (38.6 deg C) and increasing irritability with right ear pulling. He has had no vomiting and is drinking reasonably. Otoscopy of the right ear shows a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with loss of the light reflex and absent mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; the left tympanic membrane is normal.

There is no otorrhoea, no mastoid tenderness and no neck stiffness. He has no risk factors for severe AOM (not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, no cleft palate, no immunodeficiency, no cochlear implant). His mother asks whether he needs antibiotics or analgesia alone.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6°C, HR 130 bpm
data_table.Examination: Bulging, red, immobile right tympanic membrane; normal left
data_table.Investigations: None required

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnosis and management plan?

options.text: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear); reassurance, monitor hearing and arrange a routine review at 6 weeks with no antibiotic course needed
Acute otitis media; immediate amoxicillin three times daily for 5 days because antibiotics are mandatory for any AOM diagnosis under age 2
Acute otitis media, low-risk over 6 months with unilateral disease and intact TM; regular analgesia plus safety-net delayed amoxicillin prescription if not improving
Chronic suppurative otitis media; refer to ENT for tympanostomy tubes and culture-directed topical therapy with regular hearing follow-up
Otitis externa from recent swimming; commence topical ciprofloxacin drops with a wick if the canal is oedematous on otoscopy today

stem: A term infant (birth weight 3.2 kg) is now 4 hours old on the postnatal ward. He is being exclusively breastfed but his mother is concerned he is sleepy and not latching well. Bedside blood glucose is 2.2 mmol/L. He has no clinical signs of hypoglycaemia (no jitteriness, no seizure, no respiratory distress, normal tone). T 36.8 deg C, HR 140, RR 45. He is at risk because of suboptimal feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 45, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, normal tone
data_table.Investigations: BGL 2.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which combination of immediate management and threshold for escalation is most appropriate per Queensland and ANZNN paediatric guidance?

options.text: Feed breast milk (or formula if breastfeeding inadequate) AND buccal dextrose 40% gel 200 mg/kg; recheck BGL at 30 min; escalate to IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg if still under 2.6 mmol/L
Give an IV bolus of 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose immediately as first-line without trying enteral feed plus buccal gel first in this stable neonate
Observe and repeat BGL in 2 hours without specific intervention, given the absence of overt neuroglycopaenic symptoms in this neonate today
Commence IV 10% dextrose maintenance at 60 mL/kg/day without a bolus, accepting slow correction without enteral feed or buccal gel administration
Administer IM glucagon 0.1 mg/kg as first-line, deferring oral feed and buccal dextrose gel pending the glucagon-mediated glycaemic response

stem:
An 8-year-old girl with asthma on fluticasone propionate 125 mcg twice daily via MDI and spacer has been waking with cough 3 nights per week and using salbutamol 4-5 times per week for the past month. She has no daytime symptoms outside of PE class, where she takes pre-exercise salbutamol but still develops cough, chest tightness and a 25% drop in peak expiratory flow within 10 minutes of starting running.

There has been no exacerbation requiring oral prednisolone in the last 12 months. Her parents have observed her use the spacer technique correctly and her pharmacy refill record confirms adherence to fluticasone. She is afebrile and her chest is clear on auscultation today. Her growth has been on the 25th centile and stable; her parents are explicitly anxious about further increasing the ICS dose because of growth concerns.

She has known seasonal allergic rhinitis poorly controlled on intranasal fluticasone, and the family GP has asked you, the paediatric registrar, which preventer change best fits the Australian Asthma Handbook 6-11 year stepwise pathway given the exercise-induced pattern and the parental concern about ICS dose escalation.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO₂ 98%, RR 22, HR 90
data_table.Examination: Normal breath sounds, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: PEFR 85% predicted

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in her preventer therapy?

options.text: Step up to fluticasone 250 mcg twice daily (moderate-dose ICS) and pre-treat with salbutamol 10 minutes before PE
Maintain low-dose fluticasone and add montelukast 5 mg daily as preferred add-on for the exercise-induced pattern
Maintain low-dose fluticasone and add salmeterol 50 mcg twice daily (LABA) as combination therapy
Step up to high-dose fluticasone 500 mcg twice daily as monotherapy
Maintain current ICS and add a 3-day course of oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg to regain control of nocturnal symptoms

stem: A term infant born to a mother on buprenorphine for opioid dependence develops irritability, high-pitched cry, tremors, and diarrhoea at 48 hours of life. The Finnegan score is 12.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 60, Temp 37.8°C
data_table.Examination: Irritable, high-pitched cry, tremors, diarrhoea, excoriations
data_table.Investigations: Finnegan score 12 (requires treatment)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral morphine sulfate in divided doses titrated to Finnegan scores
Commence oral phenobarbital as monotherapy first-line for neonatal abstinence
Administer a single dose of IV naloxone via peripheral line
Provide supportive care only (swaddling, low stimulation, small frequent feeds, skin contact)
Commence oral clonidine six-hourly as the first-line pharmacological agent

stem: A 3-year-old girl with severe atopic dermatitis presents with a 5-day flare that has not responded to her usual topical corticosteroid (mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment twice daily) and moisturisers. Her mother reports she has been scratching intensely and not sleeping. On examination, there is extensive erythema, lichenification, and weeping of the flexural areas of both arms and legs. There are also pustules on the cheeks and perioral area. She is afebrile. The lesions are not vesicular and do not look punched-out.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.1°C, HR 100, RR 22
data_table.Examination: Weeping erythematous flexural eczema, pustules on cheeks and perioral area, no vesicles, no systemic signs
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin three times daily for secondary bacterial infection, and apply wet dressings with diluted corticosteroids
Start oral aciclovir four times daily for suspected eczema herpeticum
Prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid (e.g., betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment) and add a calcineurin inhibitor
Refer to dermatology for consideration of oral prednisolone or ciclosporin
Perform a skin swab for culture and await results before prescribing antibiotics

stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with a limp and a swollen right knee of 6 weeks' duration, worse in the morning with stiffness lasting 30 minutes. She is otherwise well, afebrile, and has no rash. The right knee is warm, swollen, and has a small effusion but is not erythematous. The left knee and other joints are normal. Investigations show: WCC 9.5 ×10⁹/L, CRP 15 mg/L, ESR 35 mm/hr, ANA positive (1:640).

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0°C, HR 95, RR 22
data_table.Examination: Swollen, warm right knee with effusion, no other joint involvement, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.5, CRP 15, ESR 35, ANA 1:640, X-ray: soft tissue swelling, no bony erosion

lead_in: What is the most important associated investigation or examination?

options.text: Slit-lamp examination by ophthalmologist to screen for chronic anterior uveitis
MRI of the right knee with intravenous gadolinium contrast enhancement
Transthoracic echocardiogram to assess for occult pericarditis or valvulitis
Anti-streptolysin O titre to exclude acute post-streptococcal rheumatic fever
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy to exclude acute leukaemia

stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with 3 months of bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain and 6 kg weight loss. She has noticed a painful perianal lump that discharges pus. On examination she is pale, BMI under the 5th centile, with a perianal fistula draining pus and no mouth ulcers. Bloods: Hb 92, CRP 58, albumin 28, faecal calprotectin over 2000 mcg/g. Colonoscopy shows recto-sigmoid inflammation with skip lesions in the caecum and deep serpiginous ulcers in the terminal ileum; biopsies are pending. HR 105, BP 100/65, T 37.3 deg C.

data_table.Examination: Pale, thin, perianal fistula, no mouth ulcers
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92, CRP 58, albumin 28, faecal calprotectin >2000; colonoscopy: continuous recto-sigmoid inflammation, skip lesions caecum, terminal ileal ulcers

lead_in: Which combination of most likely diagnosis and most discriminating endoscopic feature is correct?

options.text: Crohn's disease; perianal fistula together with terminal ileal involvement and skip lesions is the discriminating finding
Ulcerative colitis; perianal fistula reflects ongoing severe colitis
Infectious colitis with secondary perianal abscess
Coeliac disease with secondary anaemia
Behcet disease with intestinal involvement

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to a GP by his parents who are concerned about his language. He says only 5 single words, does not combine words, and does not point to share interest. He rarely responds to his name and spends long periods lining up his toy cars. He was born at term and walked at 14 months. His newborn hearing screen was normal. There has been no developmental regression. The GP wishes to start the developmental concern assessment pathway.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal for age
data_table.Examination: Reduced eye contact, solitary play, no pretend play, repetitive car lining
data_table.Investigations: Hearing test normal at birth

lead_in: Which combination of investigation and next-step referral is most appropriate?

options.text: Repeat formal audiology assessment AND administer the M-CHAT-R/F autism-specific screening tool; if either is abnormal, refer to a developmental paediatrician or community paediatric service via the public pathway; the AGPAR-funded diagnostic assessment requires a paediatrician or psychologist using DSM-5 criteria
Administer the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3) alone and reassess at age 3 if delayed
Administer the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) in the GP rooms today and provide a diagnosis
Order WPPSI cognitive assessment to establish intellectual level before any autism workup
Refer directly to a developmental paediatrician without screening because referrals are accepted on clinical concern alone

stem: A 9-year-old girl is referred by her GP with a 2-week history of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and fatigue. There is no vomiting, no abdominal pain, and she is clinically well. Blood glucose is 22 mmol/L, and ketones are 1.2 mmol/L. Venous pH is 7.35, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L. She is not dehydrated.

data_table.Examination: Mildly dry mucous membranes, no dehydration, alert
data_table.Investigations: BGL 22 mmol/L, ketones 1.2, pH 7.35, HCO₃⁻ 20

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial insulin regimen?

options.text: Commence subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin (e.g., insulin glargine once daily plus insulin aspart before meals) with age-appropriate carbohydrate counting education and diabetes team involvement
Start an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour until blood glucose is below 10 mmol/L, then transition to subcutaneous insulin
Prescribe oral metformin 500 mg BD to improve insulin sensitivity and delay insulin requirement
Administer a single dose of subcutaneous insulin glargine 0.3 units/kg and monitor for 24 hours
Start a twice-daily premixed insulin (e.g., 30/70)

stem:
A 3-week-old male infant presents with a 4-day history of progressively worsening non-bilious vomiting, now projectile after every feed. He is alert but appears dehydrated with sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. His weight is 3.4 kg, down from a birth weight of 3.8 kg. A test feed reveals a palpable 'olive-shaped' mass in the right upper quadrant and visible gastric peristalsis.

Venous blood gas shows: pH 7.49, pCO₂ 46 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L, chloride 89 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160 bpm, BP 70/45 mmHg, RR 44, Temp 36.9°C
data_table.Examination: Dehydrated, sunken eyes, dry mucosae, palpable olive mass RUQ, visible peristalsis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid for correcting the dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose and 20 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance rate
Hartmann's (Ringer's lactate) solution at 1.5 times maintenance rate via peripheral IV cannula
0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg boluses until perfusion improves, then 0.9% saline plus 5% dextrose
0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose and 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance rate
5% dextrose with 0.2% sodium chloride at twice maintenance rate via peripheral IV cannula

stem:
A term female infant is born to a 32-year-old mother with SLE and known anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies. At 2 hours of age, an annular erythematous rash is noted on the face and scalp. Heart rate is 70 bpm and regular; she is pink, well-perfused and in no respiratory distress. ECG shows third-degree AV block with atrial rate 140, ventricular rate 70 and narrow QRS.

Bedside echo shows normal cardiac anatomy and good biventricular function; there is no hydrops. BP 65/35, SpO2 96 percent on room air. There are no clinical signs of low cardiac output.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70 bpm (ventricular), RR 45, SpO₂ 96% RA, BP 65/35 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Erythematous annular rash face/scalp, bradycardia, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: ECG: complete AV block, atrial rate 140, ventricular rate 70, narrow QRS; Echo: normal anatomy, good function; maternal anti-Ro/SSA positive

lead_in: Which combination of immediate management and longer-term plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Empirical IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg to clear maternal autoantibodies and reverse the conduction block in this currently asymptomatic neonate
Admit for continuous cardiac monitoring with PICU input; do NOT pace acutely as he is asymptomatic with adequate escape; pacemaker if rate falls under 50-55 bpm or low output
Oral prednisolone daily to suppress autoimmune injury to the conduction system, continued for at least 6 months until maternal antibodies clear from circulation
Observe without specific monitoring as the block typically resolves in 6 months once maternal autoantibodies clear from neonatal circulation completely
Insert a temporary transvenous pacemaker immediately, targeting a ventricular rate of 100 bpm

stem: A 4-year-old boy was diagnosed with Kawasaki disease on day 8 of fever. He received intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion and high-dose aspirin 30 mg/kg/day. The fever defervesced within 48 hours, and he was transitioned to low-dose aspirin 3 mg/kg/day. A follow-up echocardiogram at 3 weeks shows a giant aneurysm of the left anterior descending artery measuring 8 mm in diameter (z-score +10) and a smaller aneurysm of the right coronary artery (4 mm, z-score +4).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg, Temp 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well, no mucocutaneous signs, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: Echo: giant LAD aneurysm 8 mm (z +10), RCA aneurysm 4 mm (z +4); Plt 350; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most important additional medication?

options.text: Add clopidogrel to dual antiplatelet therapy
Add warfarin with a target INR of 2.0-3.0 in addition to low-dose aspirin
Increase aspirin dose back to high-dose as monotherapy is sufficient for thromboprophylaxis
Administer a second dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg to accelerate aneurysm resolution
No additional medication; low-dose aspirin alone is sufficient for giant aneurysms

stem: A 3-month-old female presents to ED with fever (38.6 deg C), irritability and poor feeding for 24 hours. She has no cough, rash or focal infection. Bag urine on the ward showed nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase 3+ and white cells over 100 x 10^6/L. The on-call paediatric registrar is reviewing the next step. The infant is irritable, has a normal fontanelle, and HR 170, RR 44, SpO2 97 percent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6°C, HR 170 bpm, RR 44, SpO₂ 97%
data_table.Examination: Irritable, no focus of infection, normal fontanelle
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: nitrites+, LE 3+, WBC >100 ×10⁶/L

lead_in: Which combination of confirmatory sampling, empirical therapy and imaging is most appropriate?

options.text: Commence oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole based on the bag urine and arrange outpatient renal ultrasound within the next 6 weeks of presentation
Catheter (or SPA) urine for culture before antibiotics; admit and commence IV benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) plus IV gentamicin; arrange renal ultrasound during admission
Trust the bag urine and commence IV antibiotics immediately without obtaining a sterile catheter or SPA specimen first in this febrile neonate
Treat with antipyretics and review in 24 hours, attributing the febrile illness to a presumed viral cause
Perform lumbar puncture before any antibiotics in this febrile neonate as the first procedural step

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-month history of excessive thirst and frequent urination, including nocturia. He drinks 4-5 L of water per day. His serum sodium is 148 mmol/L, serum osmolality 305 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality is 150 mOsm/kg. After 4 hours of water deprivation, his serum osmolality rises to 310 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality remains at 160 mOsm/kg. After administration of subcutaneous desmopressin, urine osmolality increases to 650 mOsm/kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 90 bpm, BP 100/60 mmHg, RR 20
data_table.Examination: Normal, no signs of dehydration
data_table.Investigations: Serum Na 148, serum Osm 305, urine Osm 150; after water depr: serum Osm 310, urine Osm 160; after desmopressin: urine Osm 650

lead_in: What type of diabetes insipidus does this child have?

options.text: Central (cranial) diabetes insipidus
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Primary polydipsia (psychogenic polydipsia)
Diabetes mellitus
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH)

stem: A 6-year-old boy with palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks, colicky abdominal pain, and knee swelling presents with 3+ protein and 3+ blood on urine dipstick. His blood pressure is 112/72 mmHg (90th centile). He is otherwise well. Spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) is 280 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/72 (90th centile), HR 95 bpm
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura lower limbs, swollen knees, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Urine: 3+ protein, 3+ blood; UPCR 280 mg/mmol; serum creatinine 50 µmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology for consideration of renal biopsy and possible immunosuppressive therapy
Discharge with oral prednisolone daily and a follow-up urine dipstick in 1 week
Start an ACE inhibitor (enalapril) and monitor urine protein weekly
Reassure that the renal involvement is mild and will resolve spontaneously
Order a renal ultrasound and voiding cystourethrogram

stem: A 9-month-old boy presents with intermittent colicky abdominal pain, red-currant-jelly stool and a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound confirms an ileocolic intussusception. He is haemodynamically stable (HR 150, BP 85/55, RR 36, T 37.2 deg C), afebrile and has a soft abdomen without peritonism. IV fluid resuscitation is running. Abdominal x-ray shows no pneumoperitoneum. There is no evidence of small-bowel perforation. Paediatric surgery is on standby. The radiology team is available for fluoroscopic-guided reduction.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150 bpm, BP 85/55 mmHg, RR 36, Temp 37.2°C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no peritonism, palpable mass RUQ
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: ileocolic intussusception; AXR: no free air

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate definitive management and what is the safety prerequisite for that procedure?

options.text: Non-surgical reduction by air enema under fluoroscopic guidance, with paediatric surgery on standby; proceed only if peritonitis, perforation, or shock are ABSENT
Emergency laparotomy with manual reduction as first-line, bypassing imaging and non-operative options regardless of clinical stability
Observation with serial abdominal examinations only, deferring all imaging and intervention pending presumed spontaneous resolution over hours
Diagnostic laparoscopy and laparoscopic reduction as first-line, bypassing non-operative air enema in this clinically stable child without imaging
IV antibiotics and bowel rest alone, treating as presumed gastroenteritis without addressing the obstructing lesion or arranging imaging

stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to the ED by her parents after they discovered she ingested approximately 50 tablets of paracetamol 500 mg (total 25 g) following an argument at school. The ingestion occurred approximately 10 hours ago. She complains of nausea and mild right upper quadrant discomfort. She weighs 45 kg. She is alert and oriented with slight epigastric tenderness.

HR 100, BP 105/65, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent, T 36.9 deg C. A paracetamol level drawn 9 hours post-ingestion is 1800 micromol/L. ALT 45 U/L, AST 50 U/L, total bilirubin 18, INR 1.1, creatinine 60. She has no known medical history and no other ingestions.

data_table.Examination: Alert, mild RUQ tenderness, no jaundice, no encephalopathy
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol level 1800 µmol/L at 9h; ALT 45, AST 50, bilirubin 18, INR 1.1, Cr 60

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Commence IV N-acetylcysteine using the AU two-bag regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours) without nomogram comparison given dose >200 mg/kg
Activated charcoal 50 g orally now and reassess the need for NAC at 4 hours
Observe without treatment as ALT and INR are currently normal; repeat bloods at 12 hours to detect delayed hepatotoxicity before considering NAC initiation
Refer immediately for liver transplantation evaluation on the basis of the paracetamol level alone
IV pantoprazole 40 mg for gastric protection and immediate psychiatric review without addressing the paracetamol toxicity itself through NAC therapy

stem: A term infant is born by emergency caesarean section for suspected placental abruption. Apgars are 2 at 5 minutes and 4 at 10 minutes. Cord blood pH is 6.85, base deficit 18 mmol/L. At 2 hours of age, the infant is hypotonic, has intermittent apnoea, and a weak cry. Neurological examination shows reduced consciousness, decreased spontaneous movements, and an absent suck reflex. The infant meets criteria for moderate hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) by clinical staging. Amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) shows moderately abnormal background activity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120 bpm, BP 55/30 mmHg, RR assisted, SpO₂ 95%
data_table.Examination: Hypotonic, reduced consciousness, absent suck, intermittent apnoea
data_table.Investigations: Cord pH 6.85, BD 18; aEEG moderately abnormal; no seizures on aEEG

lead_in: What is the most appropriate core temperature target and duration?

options.text: Cool to 33.5 deg C (range 33-34 deg C) for 72 hours, followed by slow rewarming at 0.5 deg C per hour
Cool to 32 deg C for 24 hours, then actively rewarm over 6 hours
Provide only supportive care with maintenance of normothermia (36.5-37.5 deg C), as cooling is not indicated for moderate HIE
Cool to 34.5 deg C for 48 hours and reassess neurological status before continuing
Administer intravenous phenobarbital and maintain normothermia, as seizures are the primary concern

stem: A 12-year-old girl with known ileocolonic Crohn's disease on oral azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day and mesalazine presents with a 2-week history of painful perianal swelling and purulent discharge. She has no abdominal pain or diarrhoea. Examination reveals an indurated perianal fistula with expressible pus. A pelvic MRI confirms a transsphincteric fistula with an associated small abscess.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 85 bpm, BP 110/65 mmHg, Temp 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Perianal fistula with purulent discharge, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: MRI: transsphincteric fistula, small abscess; CRP 35 mg/L; Hb 105 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management in addition to antibiotics and surgical drainage?

options.text: Commence TNF inhibitor infliximab IV at 0, 2, and 6 weeks, then 8-weekly, with continued immunomodulator
Increase azathioprine dose and continue mesalazine, expecting the fistula to heal with medical therapy alone
Perform a fistulotomy with primary closure under general anaesthesia and continue current azathioprine
Insert a Seton drain and treat with oral metronidazole three times daily for 6 months
Refer for diverting colostomy as perianal Crohn's disease is refractory to all medical therapy

stem: An 18-month-old boy has 24 hours of vomiting and lethargy, then a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He had a viral illness 3 days ago and has been eating poorly. He is obtunded and has been intubated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160 /min, BP 90/60 mmHg, RR 40 /min and deep, T 37.8 degrees C, GCS 7
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 420 micromol/L, pH 7.48, pCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, glucose 5.5 mmol/L, normal LFTs, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological therapy to lower the ammonia level?

options.text: Sodium benzoate and phenylacetate, with arginine
Lactulose 10 mL hourly by nasogastric tube
N-acetylcysteine as a hepatoprotective agent
Haemodialysis alone, with no scavenging drug
Oral neomycin to suppress ammonia-producing flora

stem:
A 7-year-old girl with genetic generalised epilepsy presents with convulsive status epilepticus. She received buccal midazolam 0.5 mg/kg 20 minutes ago without effect, then IV levetiracetam 40 mg/kg 15 minutes ago with ongoing seizures. She has now been convulsing continuously for 45 minutes. IV access is established and she is intubated and ventilated by the ED team. BP 90/55, HR 130, SpO2 96 percent.

BGL 6.0, Na 138, ionised calcium normal. CT brain performed earlier is normal. There is no eclampsia, no hyponatraemia and no hypoglycaemia. The paediatric neurologist is unavailable and PICU is preparing to admit.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 90/55, HR 130, ventilated, SpO₂ 96%
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure ongoing, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: BGL 6.0, Na⁺ 138, Ca²⁺ normal, CT brain (performed earlier) normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next anticonvulsant under the APLS Australia status epilepticus pathway?

options.text: IV midazolam infusion titrated to seizure suppression with PICU monitoring; consider thiopentone or phenobarbital if midazolam ineffective
IV phenytoin loading 20 mg/kg over 20 minutes as third-line therapy with cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias and infusion-site irritation
IV propofol bolus then prolonged infusion in this non-intubated child without dedicated anaesthetic support or airway readiness
Intramuscular paraldehyde as the next-line anticonvulsant via the existing peripheral IV cannula
IV magnesium sulfate 40 mg/kg over 20 minutes as the next-line anticonvulsant for refractory status

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with generalised oedema, weight gain, and frothy urine of 10 days' duration. Urine dipstick shows 4+ protein, and a spot protein-to-creatinine ratio is 320 mg/mmol. Blood tests show serum albumin 18 g/L, creatinine 55 µmol/L, and total cholesterol 8.5 mmol/L. There is microscopic haematuria (+++ on dipstick), but no visible blood. Blood pressure is 118/80 mmHg (95th centile). Complement C3 level is low at 0.3 g/L (normal 0.9-1.8). Antinuclear antibody is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/80 (95th centile), HR 90 bpm
data_table.Examination: Oedematous, no rash, no arthritis
data_table.Investigations: Urine: 4+ protein, PCR 320 mg/mmol, +++ haematuria; Albumin 18 g/L, Cr 55 µmol/L, cholesterol 8.5; C3 0.3 g/L, ANA negative

lead_in: Which feature most strongly indicates the need for a renal biopsy before starting corticosteroids?

options.text: Low serum complement C3 level
Microscopic haematuria
Age of 10 years
Blood pressure at the 95th centile
Nephrotic-range proteinuria (PCR >200 mg/mmol)

stem: A 4-week-old male infant with projectile non-bilious vomiting has ultrasound-confirmed hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. He was clinically dehydrated on arrival. Initial VBG: pH 7.52, pCO2 46, HCO3 34, Cl 82, Na 130, K 3.2. He received 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus and is now on 0.9% saline plus 5% dextrose plus 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance. Twenty-four hours later: Cl 96, HCO3 27, urine output adequate. The surgical registrar is preparing for Ramstedt pyloromyotomy and the anaesthetist is reviewing operative readiness.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 150 bpm, BP 70/45, RR 40
data_table.Examination: Dehydrated, palpable olive mass
data_table.Investigations: Initial: pH 7.52, HCO₃⁻ 34, Cl⁻ 82, Na⁺ 130, K⁺ 3.2; after 24h: Cl⁻ 96, HCO₃⁻ 27, UOP adequate

lead_in: Which biochemical thresholds must be met before proceeding to pyloromyotomy?

options.text: Chloride over 95 mmol/L AND bicarbonate under 30 mmol/L AND potassium over 3.5 mmol/L with adequate urine output
Sodium over 135 mmol/L AND potassium over 3.5 mmol/L only, without any requirement for chloride or bicarbonate correction
Venous pH below 7.40 only, regardless of electrolyte derangement or current intravascular volume status today
Base excess below +5 only, regardless of sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate or urine output status
Normal serum creatinine alone, regardless of any acid-base, electrolyte or volume derangement currently

stem:
A term infant is born through thick meconium-stained liquor with poor respiratory effort and a heart rate of 60 bpm. The infant is placed under a radiant warmer, and the airway is suctioned with a large-bore suction catheter under direct vision. Despite this, the infant remains bradycardic with a heart rate of 60 bpm and is gasping. Positive pressure ventilation with a T-piece device is commenced.

The heart rate improves to 100 bpm after 30 seconds of effective ventilation. The infant begins to breathe spontaneously but remains cyanotic with an SpO₂ of 70% on air.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100 bpm, SpO₂ 70%, respiratory effort present
data_table.Examination: Thick meconium, suctioned, now breathing, cyanotic
data_table.Investigations: None

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue positive pressure ventilation with supplemental oxygen, titrating FiO2 to achieve target SpO2 of 80-85% by 5 minutes
Perform immediate tracheal intubation and suction the trachea for meconium before continuing ventilation
Commence chest compressions as the next escalation step based on the persistent low SpO2
Administer intravenous adrenaline at the neonatal resuscitation dose as the infant remains cyanotic
Provide blow-by oxygen at 10 L/min and observe, as the heart rate is above 100 bpm and the infant is breathing

stem: A 7-year-old boy with new-onset T1DM is being treated for severe DKA with IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/hr and IV 0.9% saline. Initial: pH 6.98, HCO3 4, glucose 32, ketones over 6. After 4 hours: glucose 18, pH 7.12, HCO3 7, ketones 4.5. He has received 1.5 L of 0.9% saline. He suddenly develops a severe headache, becomes bradycardic (HR 55), hypertensive (BP 130/90), and his GCS drops from 15 to 9. Pupils are equal but sluggish. Na 130, K 4.8. Glucose remains 18 (NOT hypoglycaemia).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 55 bpm, BP 130/90, RR irregular, SpO₂ 96%, GCS 9
data_table.Examination: Sudden headache, bradycardia, hypertension, deteriorating consciousness
data_table.Investigations: Na⁺ 130, K⁺ 4.8, glucose 18, pH 7.12, HCO₃⁻ 7, ketones 4.5
data_table.Medications: IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/hr, 0.9% NaCl at 1.5x maintenance

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: IV 3% hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg over 10-20 minutes OR IV mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg; reduce IV fluid rate by one-third; arrange urgent CT and PICU input
Stop insulin, give 2 mL/kg of 50% dextrose IV and IV hydrocortisone 50 mg without addressing the raised intracranial pressure or cerebral oedema
Intubate immediately and hyperventilate to pCO2 25-30 mmHg as a primary intervention to lower intracranial pressure in this child today urgently
Increase 0.9% saline rate to 20 mL/kg/hour to improve cerebral perfusion
Reduce insulin to 0.05 units/kg/hour and continue current fluid management without any specific neuroprotective intervention at this point today

stem: A 16-year-old girl with severe anorexia nervosa and BMI 14 presents with 4 weeks of postprandial epigastric pain, early satiety and bilious vomiting; she has lost a further 3 kg. Examination: scaphoid abdomen, visible aortic pulsation and succussion splash. Upper GI contrast: dilated proximal duodenum with abrupt linear cut-off at the third part. CT angiography: aortomesenteric angle 6 degrees (normal 28-65). She is haemodynamically stable. BP 90/60, HR 100. She has no other identified GI disease.

data_table.Examination: Scaphoid abdomen, visible aortic pulsation, succession splash
data_table.Investigations: UGI: dilated duodenum, linear cut-off; CT: aortomesenteric angle 6°

lead_in: Which combination of diagnosis and management plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome from severe weight loss; nasojejunal feeds with cautious eating-disorder team refeeding
Chronic duodenal atresia with neonatal-onset bilious vomiting and a high duodenal cut-off on contrast
Annular pancreas causing congenital duodenal compression in infancy with chronic feeding intolerance
Eosinophilic oesophagitis with dysphagia, food impaction and ringed oesophageal mucosa endoscopically
Median arcuate ligament syndrome causing post-prandial coeliac artery compression and epigastric pain

stem: A 6-week-old term infant presents with persistent jaundice and acholic stools since 3 weeks of age. Total bilirubin is 160 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 100 µmol/L, AST 150 U/L, GGT 1200 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound shows an absent gallbladder after a 4-hour fast and the 'triangular cord' sign. A hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan after phenobarbital priming shows no tracer excretion into the bowel at 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal for age
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced, pale stools, liver 2 cm below RCM
data_table.Investigations: Conjugated bili 100, GGT 1200, USS absent GB, triangular cord sign, HIDA no excretion

lead_in: What is the most critical factor for prognosis?

options.text: Performing the Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of age
Pretreatment with ursodeoxycholic acid for 2 weeks before surgery
Administration of intravenous immunoglobulin
Liver biopsy before surgery to confirm the diagnosis
Genotyping to identify the specific gene mutation

stem: A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents with a 2-day history of fever, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. He has been hospitalised for a pain crisis affecting his arms and legs. His oxygen saturation is 88% on room air, and a chest X-ray shows a new infiltrate in the right lower lobe. Despite initiation of intravenous antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and incentive spirometry, his SpO₂ drops to 85% on 4 L of oxygen, and his respiratory rate increases to 45. Haemoglobin is 65 g/L (baseline 80 g/L), and reticulocyte count is low.

data_table.Vital signs: SpO₂ 85% on O₂, RR 45, HR 130
data_table.Examination: Pleuritic pain, right-sided crackles
data_table.Investigations: Hb 65 (baseline 80), reticulocytopenia, CXR: new infiltrate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an exchange transfusion to reduce the percentage of haemoglobin S and improve oxygenation
Administer a simple top-up transfusion of packed red blood cells
Start hydroxycarbamide (hydroxycarbamide) daily
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg
Increase oxygen flow and continue observation

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to ED after being struck by a car. He was intubated on scene for GCS 5 (E1V2M2) with a left fixed dilated pupil. On arrival BP 85/50, HR 140, SpO2 98 percent on ventilation. Non-contrast CT shows a large left subdural haematoma with 8 mm midline shift, effaced basal cisterns and early uncal herniation. The neurosurgical team is 20 minutes away by retrieval. He has decerebrate posturing on the right and the left pupil remains fixed at 6 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 85/50, HR 140, GCS 5T, left fixed dilated pupil, ventilated SpO₂ 98%
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive, left pupil 6 mm fixed, right 4 mm reactive, decerebrate posturing
data_table.Investigations: CT: large left subdural, midline shift 8 mm, uncal herniation, effaced cisterns

lead_in: Which medical intervention is most appropriate to reduce ICP while awaiting transfer, AND why is it preferred over the alternative osmotherapy in this context?

options.text: IV 3% hypertonic saline 5 mL/kg over 10-20 minutes (preferred over mannitol in hypotension), with normocapnia and head-up positioning
IV mannitol 1 g/kg over 20 minutes as the primary osmotherapy agent
Immediately hyperventilate to pCO2 25-30 mmHg as the primary intervention to reduce intracranial pressure ahead of any osmotherapy
Insert ICP monitor and start barbiturate (thiopentone) coma immediately before any osmotic agent or definitive neurosurgical intervention
IV dexamethasone to reduce cerebral oedema from his traumatic brain injury as the first-line measure ahead of osmotherapy or imaging

stem: A 5-year-old girl is admitted with a 5-day history of fever, cough, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Chest X-ray shows a right lower lobe consolidation with a moderate-sized pleural effusion. She is commenced on intravenous ampicillin. Despite 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics, she remains febrile at 39.0°C, and chest ultrasound reveals a loculated pleural effusion with septations and anechoic fluid. A chest drain is inserted, but only 50 mL of purulent fluid is drained.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.0°C, HR 130, RR 35, SpO₂ 92% RA
data_table.Examination: Right-sided crackles, reduced breath sounds, bronchial breathing
data_table.Investigations: CXR: RLL consolidation, effusion; US: loculated effusion with septations, chest drain placed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intrapleural urokinase 10,000 units in 30 mL normal saline twice daily via the chest drain
Proceed directly to VATS for decortication and drainage under general anaesthesia
Change antibiotics to intravenous cefotaxime and metronidazole and continue observation for a further 48 hours
Insert a second chest drain in the posterior axillary line under ultrasound guidance
Administer oral prednisolone daily for 5 days to reduce inflammation

stem: A 12-year-old boy with known peanut allergy develops anaphylaxis within minutes of ingesting a cookie containing peanut. He received intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg twice (5 minutes apart), intravenous normal saline boluses (total 60 mL/kg), and an intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min, which has been titrated to 0.5 mcg/kg/min. Despite this, he remains hypotensive at 70/40 mmHg, tachycardic at 150 bpm, and has cold, mottled extremities with an SpO₂ of 85% on high-flow oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 70/40, HR 150, SpO₂ 85% ventilated, mottled
data_table.Examination: Ventilated, cold extremities, no urticaria now, poor perfusion
data_table.Investigations: Normal glucose, electrolytes; pH 7.15, lactate 6 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Adrenaline infusion 0.5 mcg/kg/min, IV fluids, IM adrenaline x2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous methylene blue 2 mg/kg over 20 minutes as primary rescue without escalating other vasopressor or specialist support

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his mother saw him swallow a 20 mm button battery from a remote control 30 minutes ago. He is currently asymptomatic, alert, and tolerating his saliva. Vital signs are normal. A chest X-ray shows a round radio-opaque object in the oesophagus at the level of the thoracic inlet with a double-ring sign.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, RR 24, SpO₂ 98%, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no drooling, normal breath sounds, no stridor
data_table.Investigations: CXR: 20 mm button battery in oesophagus, double-ring sign

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer honey (or sucralfate) 10 mL orally to coat the battery and arrange urgent endoscopy for removal within 2 hours
Observe in the emergency department for 6 hours and repeat X-ray to ensure passage into the stomach
Induce vomiting with ipecac syrup to expel the battery
Administer intravenous glucagon 0.5 mg to relax the oesophagus and allow passage
Give a carbonated beverage to drink to push the battery into the stomach

A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of high fever (daily maximum 39.5°C), conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, abdominal pain, vomiting, and a diffuse maculopapular rash on his trunk. His parents report that he had a mild febrile illness with cough 4 weeks ago from which he recovered fully. On examination, he is irritable, tachycardic at 140 bpm, hypotensive at 80/50 mmHg, with cool extremities and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds.

He has bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue, and swollen hands and feet. There is no lymphadenopathy. An echocardiogram shows moderate left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 38% and mild mitral regurgitation. Laboratory tests show: white cell count 2.8 ×10⁹/L with lymphopenia (0.5 ×10⁹/L), platelets 85 ×10⁹/L, C-reactive protein 280 mg/L, ferritin 1200 mcg/L, troponin I 850 ng/L, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) 15,000 pg/mL, D-dimer 4.5 mg/L, and hypoalbuminaemia 22 g/L. SARS-CoV-2 serology is positive for IgG.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.2°C, HR 140, BP 80/50, CRT 4 sec, SpO₂ 94%
data_table.Examination: Irritable, conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue, rash, swollen hands/feet, no lymphadenopathy, cool extremities
data_table.Investigations: WCC 2.8, lymph 0.5, Plt 85, CRP 280, ferritin 1200, troponin I 850, NT-proBNP 15,000, D-dimer 4.5, albumin 22; Echo: LVEF 38%, mild MR; SARS-CoV-2 IgG positive

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C); administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and intravenous methylprednisolone daily, with vasoactive support for shock
Kawasaki disease shock syndrome; administer IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin daily, and commence a heparin infusion for coronary artery thrombosis
Septic shock of bacterial origin; obtain blood cultures and commence broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefotaxime, vancomycin, clindamycin) and a noradrenaline infusion, deferring immunomodulatory therapy
Acute rheumatic fever; commence benzathine penicillin G 900 mg IM, oral prednisolone, and aspirin
Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH); commence the HLH-2004 protocol with etoposide, dexamethasone, and ciclosporin

stem: A 14-year-old girl with ileocolonic Crohn's disease has been in clinical remission on maintenance infliximab 5 mg/kg every 8 weeks plus azathioprine 1.5 mg/kg/day. Over the past 3 months she has developed abdominal pain, 4-5 loose stools per day and a rising faecal calprotectin from 50 to 850 mcg/g. She is due for her infliximab infusion today. Pre-infusion bloods: infliximab trough under 1 mcg/mL (therapeutic over 3), anti-infliximab antibodies (ATI) HIGH at 120 ng/mL, CRP 35, albumin 30. There is no perianal disease and no surgical emergency. She has no contraindications to anti-TNF or methotrexate.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 85, BP 110/65, Temp 36.9°C, weight 45 kg
data_table.Examination: Mild RLQ tenderness, no perianal disease
data_table.Investigations: Infliximab trough <1, anti-infliximab antibodies 120, faecal calprotectin 850, CRP 35, albumin 30

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step given the therapeutic drug monitoring result?

options.text: Switch to adalimumab (second anti-TNF) with loading 160/80 mg at 2 weeks then 40 mg fortnightly AND add immunomodulator (methotrexate or continued azathioprine) to reduce immunogenicity
Increase infliximab to a higher dose every 4 weeks as dose intensification of the current biologic
Switch directly to ustekinumab as an out-of-class agent without trialling a second anti-TNF biologic first
Add oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and continue the same infliximab regimen unchanged
Stop all biologic therapy and refer for elective colectomy as the next definitive step

A 14-year-old previously well girl presents with a 4-week history of progressive psychiatric symptoms. Initially, she became anxious, withdrawn, and developed insomnia. Over the past week, she has developed rapid, jerky speech, orofacial dyskinesias, and episodes of agitation alternating with catatonic posturing. She has had three generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the past 24 hours. On examination, she has autonomic instability with labile blood pressure (ranging 160/100 to 90/50), tachycardia, and hyperthermia (38.3°C).

She exhibits florid orofacial and limb dyskinesias, echolalia, and periods of mutism. MRI brain with contrast is normal. Lumbar puncture shows mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (WCC 25 ×10⁶/L, predominantly lymphocytes), normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein. Electroencephalogram shows extreme delta brush pattern. Serum and CSF anti-NMDA receptor antibodies are strongly positive. A pelvic ultrasound reveals a 5 cm right ovarian teratoma.

data_table.Vital signs: BP labile, HR 120-150, Temp 38.3°C, RR 20-30
data_table.Examination: Orofacial and limb dyskinesias, echolalia, mutism, catatonic posturing, autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: CSF: 25 WCC, lymphocytic; EEG: extreme delta brush; anti-NMDAR antibodies positive; Pelvic USS: 5 cm ovarian teratoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days plus IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days, urgent laparoscopic oophorectomy
Start oral risperidone 2 mg twice daily for psychosis and schedule routine outpatient psychiatric review next week
Initiate IV aciclovir 8-hourly for presumed herpes simplex CNS infection until CSF PCR returns
Perform therapeutic plasma exchange alone as sole immunomodulatory therapy, without corticosteroids, to avoid psychiatric worsening
Administer intravenous rituximab weekly for 4 weeks as the first-line immunomodulatory therapy

stem: A 13-year-old previously well girl presents with a 2-week history of jaundice, malaise, and abdominal distension. On examination, she is icteric, has ascites, and the liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin with a firm edge. Laboratory tests show: total bilirubin 280 µmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 180 µmol/L, alanine aminotransferase 95 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 120 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 85 U/L (low for age), international normalised ratio 3.5, albumin 22 g/L, haemoglobin 85 g/L, reticulocytes 12%, direct Coombs test negative.

data_table.Examination: Icteric, ascites, firm hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp (pending)
data_table.Investigations: Bili 280/180, ALT 95, AST 120, ALP 85, INR 3.5, albumin 22, Hb 85, retic 12%, Coombs negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most useful diagnostic test?

options.text: Wilson disease with acute liver failure and Coombs-negative haemolysis; check ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper
Autoimmune hepatitis; test for ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, and liver-kidney microsomal type 1 antibody
Acute paracetamol toxicity; send serum paracetamol level and commence N-acetylcysteine without delay
Hepatitis A infection; test serum hepatitis A IgM antibodies and arrange supportive care
Budd-Chiari syndrome; arrange Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins for confirmation
